WEAVING THE WEB OF LIFE. "This morn I will weave my web," she said, As she stood by her loom in the rosy light, And her young eyes, hopefully glad and clear, Followed:afar the swallow's flight. "As soon as the day's first tasks are done, While yet I am fresh aid strong'? Oak) kuln "I will hasten to weave the beautiful web f Whose pattern is known to none but me.

• "I will weave it fine, I will weave it fair, And ah I how the colours will glow," she said. • ":So fadeless and strong I will weave my web, \ That perhaps it will live after I am dead." But the morning hours sped on apace; • The air grew sweet with the breath of June And young Love hid by the waiting loom. Tangled the threads as he hummed a tune. ' "Ah ! Life is so rich and full," she cried, "And morn is short, though the days are long! This noon I will weave my beautiful web. I will weave it carefully, fine and s'trong." But the sun rode high in the cloudless sky The burden and heat of the 4637 she bore;

And hither and thither she cagier-and went, While the loom stood still as it stood before. "Ah! life is too busy at noon," she said; My web must wait till the eventide, Till the common work of the day is done, And my heart grows calm in the silence wider' So, one by-one, the hours passed on, Till the creeping shadows had longer grown; Mil the house was still, and the breezes slept, And her singing birds to their nests had flown. "And now I will weave my web," she said. And she turned to her loom ere set of sun, And laid her hand on the shining threads To set them in order, one by one. But hand was tired, and heart was weak; "I am not so strong as I was," sighed she, "And the pattern is blurred, and the colours rare Are not so bright, or fair to see ! "I must wait, I think, till another morn; I must go to my rest with my work undone; It is growing too dark to weave l" she cried, As lower and lower sank the sun. She dropped the shuttle; the lcom stood still; The weaver slept in the twilight gray. Dear heart! Will she weave her beautiful web In the golden light of a longer day?

Dr. Dempater, one of the most patriotic Scotchmen of his day, furnished Boswell, with many a titbit for bis note book. One of these relates to Sir Robert Walpole and a sycophantish bishop. The Bishop was flattering Sir Robert egregiously. A gentleman asked the statesman how he could bear such fulsome stuff. "Sir." replied Walpole, "if you were as severely scourged in the House of Commons as I am, you would be glad of any dog to lick your sores." Dr. Dow' of Errol, and Dr. Duff, of Kilspindle, minis- ters in the Carse of Gowrie, were both humorists, and often met. On a New Year's Day, Dr. Dew sent to his friend, who was a great snuffer, a mull, inscribed, "Dr. Dow to Dr. Duff, snuff! snuff! snuff !!" The allusion to this habit, Dr. Duff resolved pithily to avenge, and, know- ing his friend's weakness for toddy, despatched to him a hot water jug, with the lines upon the lid," Dr. Duff to Dr. Dow, fou! foul fou!!" A little school girl asked her teacher what all the folks meant when they spoke of" Mrs. Grundy." "Why, my dear," replied the teacher, "by Mrs. Grundy,' they mean the world." A day or two afterwards the.same teacher .asked the geography class to which this infantile bud of promise belonged what was meant by the term "cone." After some hesitation, the little girl spoke up, with a deal of assurance and confidence, "I know, teacher; it's the belt round Mrs. Grundy's waist." The town of Perugia having sent deputies to Urban V., who was then at Avignon, they found the pontiff sick in bed. The orator of the embassy made him a long speech, without paying any regard to his indisposition, and without ever coming to the point. When he had done, the Pope asked them whether they had anything to state. Seeing that he was heartily tired, they said, " Our instructions are to declare to your Holiness that, if you do not grant us what we ask, our orator will make his speech over again before we go." The Pope granted demand instantly. WISE SAYINGS VROH CHINA.—Here are a few Chinese eayings handed down for over two thousand years Regard faithfulness and sincerity as first principles. A good man is serene; a bad man always in fear. To see what is right and not to do it is want of courage. He who offends against Heaven has none to whom he can pray. I will not grieve at men's not knowing me; I will grieve that I do not know men. If in the Morning 7011 have heard the voice of celestial reason, in the even- ing you will be fit to die. He who devotes himself to the study of the true and the good with perseverance and without relaxation, derives therefrom great satisfaction. When we see men of worth we should think of equalling them; when we see men of a contrary character we should turn inwards and examine ourselves.—Confudats.• How To Pirr YOUR Name ON FRUIT.—Did you ever see a name printed on a growing apple, pear, or peach? No. Well, if you wish to have that pleasure, this is the way to obtain it. While the fruit yet hang.: green upon the tree, make up your mind which is the very, biggest and the most promising specimen of all. Next, cut out from thin tough paper the initials of the name of your little brother or sister or chief crony, with round specks for dots after the letters, and the letters themselves plain and thick. Then paste the letters and dots on that side of the apple which is most turned to the sun, taking care not to loosen the fruit's hold upon the stem. As soon as the apple is ripe, take off the paper cuttings, which, having shut out the reddening rays of the sun, have kept the fruit green just beneath them' so that the name or initials now show plainly. After that, bring the owner of the initials to play near the tree, and say pre- sently, " What are those queer marks on that apple up there ?" You will find this quite a pleasant way to sur- prise the very little ones, and, of course, you can print a short pet name as easily as initials. RESCUE OF A BURIED CHILD. —By an especial provi- dence a very young child was committed to my (Mary • Moffatt's) care. One Sabbath morning, while preparing for church,some of our children brought in a report that a child was heard.crying among the stones on:the side of the hill about a quarter of a mile from the house. We immediately set off to the spot. Moffat and Mr. Millen arrived there before Me, and heard its cries, but could see nothing. At length they discovered the poor babe literally buried alive and covered with stones. At this moment I arrived, and, as you will easily:conceive, was dreadfully shocked. The inhuman mother had pulled out stones to make a hole sufficient for its little body, I and then put it in and laid upon it one huge stone, the corner of which rested on its little nose and made a severe wound. Its limbs were sadly bruised with kick- ing about, and its eyes all bleared with the cold. I took it up and brought it home, fed and washed it, and dreesed its wounds, to the great astonishment of the natives. They viewed it with indifference, said the mother was a rascal, but wondered much that we should love so poor an object,lt was only about five weeks old, but very small, like one new born. It appeared that the monstrous mother, ahsiated by her own mother, had com- mitted it to its cold tomb about four o'clock the day before, where it remidned the whole night till nine o'clock in thesneorning, when we found it. It was amazing that eltill lived, as it had rained hard, and there was not an inch of covering about it; and still more that the wolf had not got it, as a wolf will tear a dead body out of the. grave if not well secured. 'The mother was an object of charity, and had been in the habit of getting food from us. Only the day before I gave her a piece of beef for a small bundle of firewood, merely out of pity, and to her mother the very day on which the crime was committed. She had reported that her child was dead, but when she heard that we had made the discovery both she and her mother fled to an- other part of the country. Thus, you see, I have an addition to my cares; and, as I knew no one to whom I could entrust it as wet nurse, I began and carried on with the spoon till I was no longer able to do it on ac- count of my late trial, when I engaged a good-natured Hottentot, the wife a one of the men, to take it for a time, for which' I pay her liberally, the food and clothing Coming regularly from myself. It is coming on very well, and is considered a very pretty child. The remark- able way in which it has been brought into our family led us at once to adopt it as our own, and we have accordingly offered it m baptism a month ago, and named her Sarah Roby.--The Lives of Robert and Mary Moffat. • The Rev. James Patterson. of Philadelphia, once said, in a circle of his brethren, that he thought ministers ought to be humble and poor. "I have often prayed," said he, "that I might be kept humble • I never prayed that I might be poor—l could trust my church for that !" What is to be done with this precocious generation? A small girl, last Sunday asked us, with an air of self-con- sciousness, if we knew "why Eve never had the measles ?" We were fain te plead ignorance. "Because she'd Adam," quietly remarked the youngster, and then roared at our bewilderment. A Greek poet used often to present verses to Augustus in hope of reward. The Emperor wrote au epigram and gave it to the poet as a reward in kind. The man read it with high applause, and, pulling out a few denarii, gave them to Augustus, saying, "If I had more you should have more." Great laughter arising, the Emperor ordered a sum worthy of himself. A witty as well as a soft answer will sometimes turn away wrath. Charles Burleigh, the Abolitionist, in the midst of an anti-slavery speech was struck by a rotten egg full in the face. Pausing to wipe away the contents of the missile, he said calmly, "I have always contended that pro-slavery arguments were very unsound." The crowd roared, and he was no longer molested. A Jon Renuice.—The best anecdote of Gen. Grant which we have seen is the one related by Gen. Clinton B. risk, who says: "I was sitting with the General and others, when an officer high in rank rushed in, shouting, Oh boys, I've such a good story to tell you! There are no ladies present I believe No, but there are gentle- men present,' was the curt reply of Grant." The story , was not told.

Once, when John Kemble played Hamlet in the country, the gentleman who enacted Guildensterrr was, or imagined himself to be, a capital musician. Hamlet asks him—" Will you play upon this pipe ?" "My Lord, I cannot." "I pray you.' "Believe me, I cannot." "I do beseech you." IVO, if your Lordship insists on it, I shall do as well as I can ;" and to the confusion of Ham- let, and the great amusement of the audience, he played "God save the King." - Jamie Gibb, a country postman in Scotland, was in the habit of getting a ride now and again from a hawker who went his way. One morning, as Jamie was perched up on the top of the hawkees cart, the smith, who had just then handed a letter, remarked to the hawker:—" And noo, Robin, hoo mud; does Jamie, gie ye in the year for the ride doon sae often?" "Oh,' interposed Jamie, be- fore the hawker could reply," I gie him what I got frae you last Christmas, Me ye ken boo muckle that is." A Scotcliman and his wife were coming froin Leith to London by boat. When off the Yorkshire coast, a great storm arose, and the vessel had several narrow escapes from foundering. "Oh, Sandy," moaned his wife, "I'm na steers" o' deein', but I dinna care to dee at sea l" " Dinna think o' deein' yet," answered Sandy; "but, when yo do, ye'd better be drooned at sea than anywhaur else." "An' why, Sandy?" asked his wife. "Why?" exclaimed Sandy. " Because ye wouldna cost so muckle to bury!" Truth, like justice, mercy, and love, is infinite, and can never be exhausted. The finite man can only ap- proach it humbly, yet earnestly; and if he do this to the extent of his powers he will become a truthful and, an honourable man. If, however, he does not bring all his powers into this service, if he neglects to train his faculties of observation, of thought, of language, if he does not resist the bias of prejudice and of desire, if he does not-search for truth with energy, and use scrupu- lous care and accurate language in conveyin& it, ha can never attain to that character. M.45:N10• Amstar. INTELL/GENCE.—At the north side of Dublin there is at Clontarf a sea inlet where the water at cer- tain times of the tide is very shallow. A little stream flows under the road into the sea at this place. The bridge beneath which it passes has pretty high parapets. It was the practice among the .lads about, when the depth of water suited, to wade out and catch little flat- fish. These abound in great numbers, and liecommonly on the sea-bed. The waders went in hare-legged, and when they happened to tread upon a fish, kept the foot in position until they could stoop down and secure their prey. One of the fisherboys was one day attended by his dog, and when the intelligent creature saw the work in which his master was engaged proceeded to help him by plunging about, and whenever he felt a fish kept his paw upon it until his master should come up and lace it in his creel. --1111111111.=;- KEEP 1T TO YOURSELF.—You have trou e—your feel- ings are injured, your husband is unkind, your wife frets, your home is not pleasant, your friends do not treat you fairly, and things in general do not move plea- santly. Well, what of it? A smouldering fire can be found and extinguished; but when the coals are scat- tered, who can pick them up? Bury your sorrow. The place for sad and distrusting things is under the ground. A cut; finger is never benefited by pulling off the plaister and exposing it to somebody's eye. Tie it up and let it alone. Charity covereth a multitude of sins. Things thus covered are often covered without a scar, but once published and confided to meddling friends, there is no end to the trouble they may cause. Keep it to yourself. Troubles are transient, and when a sorrow is healed and passed, what a comfort it is to say, "No one ever knew it until the trouble was all over." Some time ago a gentleman found a large turnip in his field of the shape of a man's head, and with the resem- blance of the features of a man. Struck with curiosity, he had a cast made of it, and sent the cast to a society of phrenologists, stating that it was taken from the head of Baron Turenpourtz, a celebrated Polish Professor, and requested their opinion thereon. After sitting in judg- ment, they scientifically examined the cast, in which they declared that they had discovered an unusual prom- inence, which denoted that he was a man of acute mind and deep reasearch, that he had the organ of quick per- ception, and also of perseverance, with another that in- dicated credulity. The opinion was transmitted to the owner of the cast, with a letter, requesting as a particu- lar favour that he would send them the head. To this he politely replied that lie would willingly do so, but he was prevented, as he and his family bad eaten it the day before with their mutton at dinner. MR. GLADSTONE IN MIDLOTHIAN. LOCAL GOTPRNMENT AND TNE LAND LAWS. On Saturday, M. Gladstone spoke in the Corti Exc. Dalkeitb, before upwards of 3,000 persons. His recep. was enthusiastic in the extreme. Mr. GLA.DSTONB, who was accompanied by Mrs. Gladstone, _ . .
said be had never been what is called a Moderate Liberal, and he had never been what is called an Advanced Liberal. . .

He had always found the name of Liberal quite sufficient to, describe whatever in him was worthy of description. He' took the highest hope of the Tory party in the coming elec- tions to be that they mig'st obtain such an amount of strength as a minority as, with the assistance of a large Irish contingent, might be made into a majority—e state of things which would net be safe or honourable to the country. Ooe of the weapons which were be- ing used by the Tories was the Fair Trade delusion, but he did not know how to reconcile the appointment of the Royal Commission with Lord lddesleigh's expressed opinions on the subject of Free Trade. Touching on the question of diseatablishment, the right hon. gentleman said it would be idle to think of that great subject being added to the programme of the coming Parliament. As to the recent invention of Tory democracy, he described it as an attempt to outbeat the italicals in their own market by pushing popular opinions further than Radicals pushed them. But Tory democracy, so far from being a means of adding real strength to Toryism, was a means of adding great strength to Radicals, because those Tory democrats ought to per- ceive that whenever they accepted a Radical proposition the point upon which they meant to take their stand for their aan convenience became a new point ef departure for the Radical, upon which he founded fresh plans, fresh ex- pectations, and fresh engagements. In this connection he mentioned the diminution of Liberal strength in the House of Lords, and said that if this dwindling of the Liberal party la its highest ranks proceeded, it would make no ap- preciable difference in Liberal strength, but would make an appreciable difference in the strength of the House of Lords, and, it night be, accelerate the movement of ideas teyood their natural and legitimate order of advance. The right bon. gentleman then proceeded to sketch the work of the new Parliament, giving a first place to the question of local gov- ernment and local taxation, and expressing the opinion that local charges ought to remain,as they always bad been charge. upon property, but upon personal as well as real property. He indicated the need of another reform by pointing out that the effect of five millions of local charge having bees carried over to the Consolidated Fund was that, under the psetext of relieving the ratepayers, a million of taxation annually was carried over from the shoulders of property on to the shoulders of labour. That was not consistent with justice as between the different classes of the commu- nity, and an essential part, in his opinion, of the work of the coming Parliament would be to lay the axe to the root of that mishief. Coming to the land question, Mr. Glad- I stone directed attention to the holding nf estates in mitt- main. He said this was not the first time, in the present stagnant state of the land market, when it was easy or cafe to contemplate great and rapid changes. but it was a time when they might very justly consider tbe foundation of a policy, and he did not hesitate to say that he believed the only sound policy for the Legislature to adopt would be to root oat altogether the system of holding land in mortmain and to have all land prooerly so called held by individuals with all the motives (.4 a legitimate self-interest in its reward brought to bear upon it, instead of placing it under the negative and anomalous condition in which it was under the management of corporate bodies. These mort- main lands would afford the most valuable and unobjection- able means of selling land in such amounts and portions as might make it available fur the land-tilling °lessee of the community. In conclusion the right hon. gentleman im- pressed upon his hearers that hardly any duty could be more sacred and solemn than that now before the electors— namely, the duty of selecting the persons who were to per- form the work of the country, and upon whose good or bad performance of that work would depend whether they were or were not to aggravate the burdens of life for themselves and their children through many generations to come. Loud cheers

div.head: AN INTERESTING CEREMONY.
div.p: AN INTERESTING CEREMONY.

Mr. Gladstone on Monday handed over to the custody of the Edinburgh city authorities the ancient Market Crose, which was pulled down in 1756, and which he has had re- stored as nearly as possible to its original form at his own expense. In reply to an address from the Town Council, Mr. Gladstone said it bad long been kis desire to give soma visible and tangible record of the revival of his connection with Scotland, which should be agreeable to all, and wholly detached from the narrower associations of political party. That wish had been fulfilled. He looked back with pain to the mistaken idea of the authorities of the period above named which prompted them to destroy that cross. It oc- curred to him that their excuse must have been that they thought they were doing a patriotic act. At that time the Hanoverian succession became in Scotland finally an accom- plished fact, and the cross bad been so bound up with the history and records or the Stuarts that possibly, but er- roneously, the authoritiee may have thought that by dm troying the memorial they were taking away from the people who had smarted under the disorders and sufferings of the revolution of 1745 that which was a source of painful recollection. . It was 'always a misfortune to any country when it thought it was under the necessity of breaking down ancient traditions and effacing its memorials, and it was with great satisfaction that he had,peen permitted in some measure to repair the breach which had been made in the historical traditions of Scotland. Mr. Gladstone, later on, spoke of the good which international exhibities did in broadening the minds of working-men. THE TORY-PARNELLITE ALLIANCE. On Tuesday afternoon Mr. Gladstone addressed a meet- ing in the Music Hall, Edinburgh, supplementary to them which had been arranged for on his arrival amongst his constituency. Mr. Gladstone, who on appearing was re- ceived with cheers, was accompanied to the platform by: Mrs and Miss Gladstone, Mr. Henry Gladstone, Mr. T. R. Buchanan, aad Mr. John Cowan, chairman of the Liberal Association of Midlothian, and there was also present Mrs Goschen. In the absence of Sir John Don Wauchope, Mr. John Cowan was called to the chair, and he congratulated the electors on the fotirth opportunity of hearing Mr. Glad- stone, and expressed the hope that in a few days they would- be able to welcome him again as member of Parliament for Midlothian (Cheers.) Mr. GLADSTONE was received with enthusiastic cheering, which was continued for some minutes. He expressed at the commencement his great surprise that at this time of day there should be found in a number of Scotch coned. tuencies two Liberal candidates for one seat, with the cer- tain result that the seat would be given to a Tory. This; he said, was a disgrace to Liberalism and a public evil.. The want of unity in the Liberal party in 1874 lost them ten or twelve seats, and it was hardly credible that they were again going to make themselves the laughingstock of their enemies and of the world. If it Was too late to appeal] to the candidates, he had yet one hope, and that was in thl voters, whom he asked to support the beat and strongest of the Liberal candidates. He then referred to Lord Salis- bury's letter on Disestablishment, and complained that his lordship had misrepresented what be had said on the sub- ject. What was the meaning of this great effort to threat the Church into the foreground The quarrel in Scotland ' in reference to the election might be said to be nearly at an end. This was not agreeable to the purposes of the Tory party, and consequently in England an attempt was being. made to cry "Church, Church, Church .1," and to make the, people understand that this election, which had nothiug whatever to do with the Church of England, was really to decide the fate of the Church as an Establishment. All this anxiety of the Tories about the Church was nothing but a mere blind. It was not the Church that was in danger ; it was the land that was in danger. It was idle to talk of cheap and easy transfer and simple transactions with respect to land until wo had abolished en- tail in life estate. That was one of the main objects that the Liberal party had in view, and it struck horror into the Tory mind. The true object which lay in the hearts and minds of the Tory party was to prevent the important legislation which the Liberal party would have to propose in the ensuing Parliament. False promisee and false expCmatiens had for 30 years past at least been the main stock of the Tory party. The cry of protecting the farmer's interests was no longer available' and they had raised the cry of "The Church." The right boo. gentleman then referred tri Lord Salisbury's speech on Mon- day night, and said it showed a total change of tone. His Lordshib was now extremely sanguine as to the result of the elections, and the key to explain that change of tone was to be found in the speeches of Mr. Parnell. Lord Salis- bury never hoped before, but now he hoped and breathed. for now he had the alliance of Mr. Parnell for his purposes. Passing on to the Irish manifesto, he said Mr. Parnell had used words of the utmost rashness, and words which mul- titudes would interpret into an apology for assassination. It was an unwarrantable and very dangerous manner of using political power to call upon any class of voters to denounce as delivering over to death the conduct of a Viceroy who had done his best to execute justice and whose action had been fully sustained by a vast majority of the House of Commons. Mr. Gladstone attributed Mr. Parnell's conduct to two causes. First, he knew that, whatever he said or did, the Liberal party would be just. " lii spite of chains, imprisonment, aad death, we have the involuntary praise silently afforded us by the conduct of a man in contradiction to his own words." Then came hie desire to make terms with the Tory party at criti- cal divisions. In conclusion, Mr. Gladstone asked his hearers to store in their minds Mr. Parnell's declarations against the Liberal party, remarking that tlaey were the strongest arguments in their favour. The country had now, he said, to decide whether the great issues which had to be tried should be tried by men who had received their commis- sion from a footing of security or by men who had received it from a slippery Voting of slavish independence. (Loud cheers.) Mr. J. C. Wilson (banker) moved a vote of confidence in the right hon. gentleman, which was seconded by Mr. Bell (of Clifton Hall), and unanimously carried. Mr. Gladstone asked the meeting to accord a vote of thanks to the chairman, and the proceedings termi- nated. •

ST. HELENS EL& _ION. The first election •of a representative of the hcrough of St. Helens in the Commons House of Mrliament. took place on Wednesday, when Mr. Henry Seto:24Bl.olle Conservative candidate was elected by a majority of 57 votes over his politiced opponent, ColoneirDavid Gamble. The excitement attendant u'pon this., the first Contest was.rpturally. very Urea it 'it, iiiiiieKquestlejialble whether it has ever been equalled in tile annals of the town.

THS POLLING. The polling toolt place on Wednesday. ' Fortunately the weather was favourable, though dull, throughout the day. The total number of voters in the borough is 8,309, and were apportioned in the various polling districts as follows : Windle 1,988, Hardshaw 1,033, Eccleston 2,590, Parr 988. East Sutton 1,117, and West Sutton 595. When the poll closed at eight o'clock the ballot boxes were sealed lip, ana un,ler the charge of several police constables were conveyed to the Town Hall. In the A•eembly-roonn the Mayor (Alderman Mcßryde), Mr. T. Brewis (town clerk). and Ur. J. H. Crain (deputy town clerk) had made extensive arrangements for counting the votes, which was carried out by a staff of about 20 persons, equally appointed by each party. Shortly after eight o'clock an immense crowd had assembled in front of the Town Hall, and an hour later its numbers had swelled to from 15,000 to 20,000. Much cheering for the respective candidates was indulged in, but there was little rough or unruly behaviour. The votelf were counted three times in all, and notwithstanding the drizzling rain the large cOncourse awaited the result with feverish anxiety. At five minutes past twelve the Mayor and other officials issued from the entrance to the Hall and were received with prolonged cheers. During a lull in the cheering the Mayor stepped forward and announced the re- sult as follows : Seton-Karr Gamble .. 3,693

div.head: Majority
div.p: Majority

. - This declaration was received with immense cheering, hissing, and general uproar. A few minutes later the Mem- ber elect made his appearance, and was greeted with cheers mingled with hisses. Amid considerable uproar he was called upon to address those present. Mr. Seten-littrr, M.P., said: Electors of St. Helens. Allow me to congratulate you. (Hisses.) We have won a victory for the Conservative cause, and I congratulate you. I thank all the majority who have honoured ma with their confidence and support. (Cheers.) Our opt-orient is a most respectable townsman—(hisses and cheers)—and the only reason that we have beaten him is that he is on the wrong side. I hope I shall not only be the representative of the majority who have given me their votes, but also the minority. I desire to thank Colonel GAM- ble persontlly for the cordial manner in which he has conduMed this contest. For him I have the greatest respect. It will be my endeavour as your first member to consider the wants and interests of the whole population, and not only the majority who have honoured me with their support (Applause.) He then sailed for three cheers fc,r Colonel Gamble, which were lustily given, mingled with groans. Colonel Gamble, J.P., then stepped forward and addressed a few words, amid considerable Interruption. He said the poll was over, and they told him that he was beaten. He was sorry on his own account, but he was very much more sorry for the sake of those who had done so mush to endeavour to return to Parliament a man and principles which they thought were the best. He was again sorry for the town of St. Helens, because he would have liked it to have expressed such principles as he believed were right. He thought it had done wrong in the present case, and under perhaps peculiar circumstances which might not exist on another such occasion as that. But, at any rate, for the present, it appeared that his principles were in a minority, and he was only sorry that he and the majority of the electors differed so much. It was not a large but a small minority. though he expected a much greater minority on the other side. He thanked them for wh,it they had done, and the large number of votes they had given him. He hoped on another occasion they would be more successful in supporting the principles which be thought were right. (Cheers) The proceedings then concluded, and the large crowd gradually dispersed.
FEELING THAT HEATH WOULD BE A HAPPY RELIEF.

Thera was a wife's troubled heart and a son's saddened spirit in the home at Clay Cuss. Derbyshire, when, in the autumn of 1884. it was mournfully whispered by man to man, and from neighbour to neighbour, that the once robust and healthy Joseph Beresford had been gtven over to die. When for more than forty years one has lived as boy and man near the place of his birth, his neighbours are the most competent judges and hest witnesses touching his merite as a man of sin- cerity arid truth. Thus long has Mr. Joseph Beresford lived among the people of that village, and is vouched for by alibi. neigithours as an Intelligent, reliable, and popular citizen. Bur many years he had been, and still is. a deputy manager of the coal-mining business of that place. Mr. Beresford's late physi- cal prostration was but another striking Instance, among many constantly coming to public knowledge far beyond their immediate locality, how loternal maladies sudden', and mys- teriously develop, and the most robust of men, in the prime of life, are called to suffer the most painful affliction even unto the vergeof the grave, Until this occasion Mr. Beresford had rarely if ever koown a day of tines'. The alternations from perspiring heat several hundred yards in the bowels of the earth to the chiling blasts of winter winds on the surface, added to office duties aud the anxieties. incident to ills trust, added to the safety and welfare of his me.s. are doubtless among the principal causes to which may be attributable his ultimate physics prostration. Mr. Beresford'a first eonsclousness of bodily derangement was a pain in his side. accompanied with sickly faintnees, fol- lowed very soon by what seemed an enlaroment of the liver, as it was apparent to external observation, causing much pain and distress when he lay upon either side in bed, as though it adhered to the inner surface of his body. In the autumn of 1884 he was compelled to resign his duties and retire from his employment, saying he could stand it no longer. Then his stomach gave way—faintness, a sensatlon of all-goneness, watery mouth, nauseousness, lose of appetite—food taken would sooner or later be thrown up, undigested as when taken, and the once-powerful man became but a shadow of his former self, As he was daily and hourly growing weaker, his doctors frankly and honestly expressed their inability to do for him any more, and as their last advice recommended him to try hydropathlc treatment at a near establishment. This advice he followed, and took the hydropathic course for several weeks, but finally discovering no signs of relief for the alarming ail- ments of his stomach and liver, and still growing poorer and weaker, he abandoned all hope of living, and went home to die, saying to himself it was unwise to waste more money on his poor body; that if he had anything left after being placed neer the sod his good wife had better have it. Mr. Beresford's history from this time is best related in one of his neat and explicit business letters, condensed as a tele- gram : " Leaving the water cure establishment," he writes. "I was vary little better, but very weak, because I could not: eat anything to do me any good, for my stomach oouldn ot digest food, and my liver was as bad as ever. it is known to all my friends and neighbours what a poor creature I was. I had given myself up as an incurable—had owed to take medicine,' and only waited the end, feeling that death would tie a happy relief. Some weeks later it was suggested by a good neigh-1 bour and life-long friend—in fool he insisted—that I should try Mother Selsrel's Curative Syrup. I was very loth to do so, as had had many shillings' worth of all sorts of medicine, and all to no purpeee. It was like throwing money away. Howevel, I was notonly physically but mentally too weak to resist the positive mind and earnest entreaty of my friend, to which were joined the solicitations of my wife and son. A small bottle of the medicine was procured, and I took it. I cannot say that 1 felt any spObially good effects from it, but I was to very low that I had no right to expect much improvement from one little bottle. When it was gone another bottle appeared which took the same course under the directions, and before it was quite all gone I had al- most quite forgotten to think about my unhappy stomach. Food began to relish and act on my stomach as in former days. To my happy surprise, and to the delight of my family, I found myself improving. I then made up my mind I would stick well to the Syrup. I did so until I had taken nine bottles'. when I was ones more a well-man. I got to work again after being off about five months. I can truly say that lam cured of indigestion and liver troubles. I had for weeks abandoned all doctors' pre criptions or other medicines before I began with Seigel'• Syrup. Since about March (1884) I have not taken regularly any of the Syrup, but only ocoasiortally when I find myself getting% little out of order by reason of exposure to very damp or chilly weather. I then take a few drops, and it puts me right again at once. "Since I have tested the value Of the medicine in my own case I have recommended it to many people, and have given some of my own away for a test. as It is said, The proof of the pudding is in the eating thereof.'" Mr. Beresford relates with much pleasant humour the ex- preasions of utter astonishment of his business acquaintances at finding him at his Old place again. " What on earth cured you ?" hr. says, Is thp question asked him almost daily. Even one of his good doctors—who, he says, is his warm personal friend, and still his family physician—was wont to ask the wife, "What did fi-ally cure Joseph ?" When she modestly replied, "Mother Seigel's Syrup." " Preston, Sept. 21st, 1883. " My Dear Sir,—Your Syrup and Pills are still very popu- lar with my customers, many saying they are the best family medicines passible. " The other day a customer came for two bottles of Syrup, and said • Mother Seigel ' had saved the life of his wile, and he added, ' one of these bottles lam sending 15 miles away to a friend whole very ill, I have much faith in it.' " The sale keeps up wonderfully, in fact one would fancy almost that the people' were beginning to breakfast, dine, and sup on Mother Seigel's Syrup, the demand is so constant and the satisfaction so great. . .
dear Sir, yours faithfully. (Signed) " W. Bowiztat."

A PRESTON COTTON MILL BURNED Dowse.—Early on Thursday morning a fire broke out in the No. 2 mule room of M‘Guffog's Cotton Mill, Preston. In a short time the mill was completely destroyed. There were eeveral nar- row escapes of firemen. The mill ran 48,000 spindles, 28 pairs of mules, and employed 270 bands. The dam- age which is covered by insurance, is estimated at nearly £5O 000. _ _

;SION ANDII4SL LIBERIkLS., • HUSIASTIC PROCEEDINGS. ,The yel,,acciessful Belied rof iihktings liktuitber- 'llhes, ef7M-r Crosfield, the Liberal candiarrfor 'Warrington'' was appropriately brought to a close on Saturday by a procession and enthusiastic gathering of working-men in the Public Hall. This idemonstration was in every respects demonstration of working-men. Those who as a rule organised the meetings pf the ,Liberal party had,. not Atended to hold any imegtintt after the vary suece4stol one on Wednesday night, but the working-men members of the party, determined to Show their zeal in the cause kn the most unmistakeable manner. The pro- cessionists gathered on the vacant piece of land in Bewsey-rfad, oppoeite St. Pail's Chijra, and by three O'clock, the-time anininneed for the procession ,to move, ,there was on immense gathering in the neighbourhood. •A few minute after three a start was made, and the procession, preceded by a brass hand, marched by way of Taitners-lane, Horsemar- ket-street, Bridge-street, and ,Rylands-street, to the Public Hall. The procession was of great length, and, as usual on such occasions inWerringtort, 6 con- siderable number of factory girls formed in front of the band and gave additional 'interest and vafiety to ttiii proceedings. Two long pales *ere also carried in front of the procession, on one of which was a large loaf with the name of "Gladstone" beneath, and on the other was perched a very small quantity of the "staff of life," with the name of "Salisbury " beneath it, these being suggestive einblems of the different regimes of free trade and Protection. The doors of the Public Hall were kept closely barred till the arrival of the processionists, but whewflung open the hall was filled to excess in a shorter time than might have been thought physically possible. The audience was extremely' enthusiastic, and the various speakers, when they made a point in favour of Liberalism and against Toryism, were cheered to the echo. The chair was taken by Mr. W. Stirrup, who was supported by Mr. C. M. Percy (Labour can- didate for Ince Division)i Councillor Dixon, and Messrs. T. Birehall, T. Flood, G. Holford, J. Chalmers, W. Roberts, and a crowded platform of working- men. In the course of the meeting, Mr. W. Oros- field and the Rev. J. Yonge came to the platform, and were greeted with prolonged cheering. The CHAIRMAN, who was received with cheers, said he was proud that day to be the chairman of a meeting like that. He recollected the time when Ernest Jones came to Warrington, and they could not find a middle-class man to act as chairman for him. They came and asked him (the chairman), and he vote proud to say that he eat for Ernest Jones in Warrington on that occasion. He recollected the time when workingmen were treated in a vile manner. They were called the "swinish multitude" and the ragged crew ; but it was not so now. (Hear, hear.) ,They were abused then, and if working-men only knew their power at the present time they would assert it in the future. (Applause% ) The education question was now to the front. He was glad that Mr. Crosfield—(applause)—answered him in that re- spect to his Batisfaction. (Applause.) He could recollect the time when they had a noble charity In Warrington. (Hear, hear.) The Grammar School belonged to the work- ing claws, but was it a poor school now? ("No.") And who had robbed them of it but the Tories and Churchmen? (Hear, hear.) They would not allow anyone but a Tory or a Churchman to be a trustee. If the fund of the Grammar School of about £BOO a year, which belonged to the gutter and workhouse children was used for educating the poor, who could not afford to pay, he thought they would get a very good education. (Applause.) The man who left that fund 400 years since left it for the poor of the town, but the poor had been robbed of it, and it had been given to the rich. (Hear, hear.) They had also been robbing them of land and things of that sort. If people who had plenty of money to leave in the future would leave working-men to be the trustees, he did not think they (the working-men) would act so unfairly as the present trustees had te them. (Hear' hear.) He had no faith in those who had been rob- bing England since he was born. (Applause.) As a Catholic, he could say the Tories had always been their enemies. (Hear, hear, and a voice: "They'll never be owe better.") No. they would never be better. (Applause.) Mr. Tmomes Futon moved the first resolution. which was as follows :—" That in the opinion of this meeting it was the duty of the authorities of the borough to consult the interests of the working classes, who form the great majority of the electors, before fixing the day of poll, and that Friday would have been more suitable than Tuesday, and would have involved a far less loss of wages." Ap- plause.) They wished to expose another plot on the part of their friends the enemy. The greater bulk of the people of Warrington had to sweat and toil for their daily bread, and their interests should have been considered in a great public matter like the present. A general election was a matter that only occurred occasionally—once in six or seven years, and sometimes once in twelve months. That wire-pulling system which had been carried on in War- rington for years, had received another exhibition. (Hear, hear.) He found that the authorities of the town, instead of consulting those who had a deep and vital interest in the matter, consulted thoee who had less to lose and more to gain ; and he found that the efforts of the Liberal party were forestalled by an anticipated arrangement. (Applause.) When vested interests were at stake, that insidious method was always adopted. (Hear, hear.) The latter end of the week would have been more suitable for all classes. n was found to be suitable at the last election, and it regal- tad in a grand victory for the Liberal cause. The Liberals were then I. a position to dictate terms, and they would have bees in a similar position this time bad they been in time. It would not be wise for him to mention the names of those who were connected with the matter, although they were well known to those who were present that afternoon ;it was well understood in whose hand the responsibility res. ted. Ns inquiry was made as to which day would best suit the interwar+ of the masses. He found that through Tuesday being fixed as the day of polling he would have to lose a day's pay, and there were others who would prob- ably loge three times as much. He did not think they ought to be called up n to make that sacrifice when it could be avoided. (Hear, hear, and loud applause.) When l that arrangement was made, urgent appeals were me by ' Mr. McMinnies and others, but they were scorned, and they were told no alteration could be made—it was like the laws of the Medea and Persians it was unalterable. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) The arrangements had been made to suit the financial and other interests of certain parties 80 that they might gain by it. (Hear, hear, and loud ap- plause.) Mr. BROMLEY, in seconding the resolution, dealt with the question of Fair Trade, and put forward statistics to prove that the country was in a better condition to-day than at the time the Tories were in office. At the conclu- Men of an excellent speech he was loudly applauded. The CHAIRMAN, In putting the proposal to tbe meeting, said the two speeches they had just heard were better than some he had beard in the Council Chamber, where he had heard noodles speak. (Councillor Dixon : " That's too bad," and loud laughter and applause.) The motion was then carried unanimously by loud ac- olamation. Mr. Jour; CHALMER9 said he had been requested to move the next resolution, which was as follows :—" That this meeting pledges itself to use every legitimate means to return Mr. William Crosfield at the forthcoming election by a triumphant majority." (Cheers.) He asked them if they were going to return Mr. Crosfield? (Cries of "Yes.") He hoped that when they went to the poll on Tuesday morning next they would remember what they had said that after- noon, and prove once more that they were in favour of liberty, freedom, and progress. (Cheers.) For 40 years, up to the year 1830, the Tories governed this country with scarcely, a break. (Interruption.) He would ask them why that roan who was creating an interruption was like the present Government ? Because he wanted turning out. (Laughter.) During those 40 years they were engaged in war, and the'end of all was that their National Debt which stood at £150,000,000, was increased to £800,000,000. And what was there to show for it ? British manufactures did not rise during that time, and in 1830 they stood at £50,000,000. Trade was bad and wages were low. Trade decreased though the population increased, and be left them to guess the state the country was in at that time. Bread was also dear, meat could very seldom be got, as our ports were blocked against the foreigner coming in ; there were long working hours, and wages in a certain trade were only 12s a week. Was that the state of things new ? ("No," and cheers.) Hand-loom weavers were in a state of starva- tion, and were only earning in Oldham 4s. 61. per week, although they had to work a great number of hours each day; at Bolton the wages reached 5s sd, and the best wages were received in Manchester, namely, 6s 61. Bricklayers were paid 178 a week, masons from 103. 3d. to 18s, shoe- makers 128; and that was the state of affairs in this country when the Tories went out of office in 1830. (Cheers.) Having referred to the great depression which, he said, exists in France, Germany, and America, he asked the audience if they were going to vote for Sir Gilbert Greenall—(criee of "Na" and hisses)—who had opposed and would oppose their best interests, or for the Tories, who had never given them anything which had been of real benefit to them except it had been wrenched from them. Were they going to vote for Crosfield—(cries of "Yes," and cheers)—a man whose character would stand testing, and who from his earliest infancy had been working for the benefit of the great masses of the ceuntry ? (Cheers.) Mr. FARBER seconded the proposal in an effective speech. He said the Tories were trying to induce the Irishmen of Warrington to go against Mr. Crosfield. ("Never," and applause.) Alluding to the question of trade, he asked if Mr. George Woods was a fair trader ? (Loud cries of " No.") Was he a fair wage payer? ("No, no.") What was Mr. Woods? (Cries of "A knob-stick," and hisses.)-. Mr. Woods was ace of the principal managers at that firm at Longford which was a " knobstick-" wire shop. (Hear, hear, and hisses.) Let them have fair trade at home before they went abroad. (Loud applatise.) Mr. C. M. Fancy, on rising, was greeted with enthusias- tic applause. In coming in the train he said he had heard a conversation about Mr. Crosfield and Sir Gilbert Green- all. One of the parties In the same carriage said to a com- panion, " Have yen heard that story about Croafield at Warrington P" The other said "No, what is it ?" "Well," was the reply, "Crosfield has been in a sack for nearly a fort- night, and the other night be put his head out of tbeesack ,and said to somebody ' Has the election finished yet,' and he was told 'no,' when he put his head into the sack again."

(Laughter.) " Ah," replied the other, "but do you know ihere Sir Gilbert was ?" " No." "Well, he was at the ttom of the sack, and Crosfield was sitting on him." oars of laughter, and applause.) Mr. Percy then went on say that he bad come to the meeting that afternoon at some inconvenience, as he was on hie way to the seaside to recruit his health and strength to enable him to finish the work in which he was engaged in his own town. (Applause.) The great reason he had for refusing a very pressing invita- tion to speak in the Darwen division was because he was told that this was to be a meeting of workingmen. (A Voice: "It is.") He was, as they no doubt knew, a workingman's candidate, brought out by the workingmen of his own divi- sion, without wealth; brought out without means, brought out without influence, brought out simply because in his principes were represented the aspirations of the'great body of the workingmen of the county; and it was because this was to be a grand gathering of workingmen that he bad consented to come and say a few words to them. (Cheers,) Be was brought out in the Liberal interest, because he thought that every man who was not a traitor to himself and to the traditions of his country, if he had studied his- tory at all, and was a politician, must be a Liberal. (Hear, bear.) He did not mean to say that there were no Tory workingmen. He was sorry to say that there were too many in his own Division. He was sorry to know that there were too many in Warrington, but he hoped that, as the influence of education made itself felt in this country, the mist of ignorance surrounding Toryism would pass away, sad that workingmen would recognize that their greatness in the past, their greatness in the present, and that their hopes in the future, lay centred in the great Liberal party. (Cheers.) It was very well for lords and members of the aristocracy and their families to be Conser- vatives, because the present condition of things was all they could wish ; but they, the workingmen, who depended on their own own energies for their living, who depended on their own efforts for their existences, required that legislation I should be effected from year to year that should bring the ' condition of things more into harmony with the interests of the people. (Cheers.) If they studied the history of the past they would find that everything which had been for a ease against the people had been introduced by the Tories, everything that had been for the few against the many bad Sam introduced by the Tories; and they would find that every right they now enjoyed, every privilege they now enjoyed had been given to 1 them by the strenuous efforts of their Liberal forefathers against the strenuous efforts of a Tory opposi- tion. (Cheers.) He was told that in Warrington there were a great number of Catholics. He hoped there were. No- body bad studied the interests of the country more than the Catholics bad done, and to-day there was not a Catholic in England who would have had the power to vote for d mem- ber of Parliament if the Tories could have bad their way. For 30 years the condition of things was this—the Cath- olics had no right to sit in Parliament. They had net even a right to vote for members, but the Liberals in Parliament, and that good patriotic Irish leader out et Parliament, O'Connell, for 30 years fought the great battle of Catholic emancipation. (Cheers.) Year by year the matter was • brought into Parliament. Year by year it was opposed by Sir Robert Peel and the Duke of Wellington, until at last, In the year 182 E, the country was actually on the verge of civil war; and in consequence of the imminence of revo- lution, Sir Robert Peel and the Duke of Wellington declared that they dare not further oppose the measure. Yet there were Tories PO sunk in lies—and there never was an election since this world began in which more lies had been told upon public platforms than by the Tory party in this cam- paign—and yet the Tories told them that a Tory Perna- ment and a Tory Government had passed the Catholic Emancipation. Of course they passed it, and they would pass any mortal thing when the time came rather than lose their salaries and their offices. (Cheers) He firmly be- lieved that the very men in power at the present day would disestablish the Church of England if they thought it was neoessary to do so to remain il3 power. (Applause.) A great deal had been said that afternoon with reference to the date which had been fixed for the election, namely, Tuesday next. He was not surprised that tricks had been adopted by the Tory party. They would not be a Tory party if they did not play these tricks. (Hear, hear.) Mr. WILLIAX CIIO6FIXIM, who was greeted with rounds of applause on rising to address the meeting, said :—Mr. Chairman, fellow working-men—(a laugh)—did that gentle- man say I was not a working-man ? (A voice: 'No, he said ' Crosield for ever,'" and laughter.) If you think I mu not, just turn to and take five weeks at a contested elec- tion, and see whether that is not work. (Laughter and em- planes.) I have been at it now for five weeks. The work is very pleasant, but it is hard. It has been pleasant because I have bad so lunch help. I have had great help from your late msmieer—(hear. hear, and applause)—and from every- one of you working-men. I have had great help from the ladies of Warrington. Our friend in the front of the gallery (alluding to a young woman who had manifested especial enthusiasm) has been helping me at several (..t oar public meetings, and the ladies have been helpine us in their own homes. I have been going about—they said I was a stranger when I came—but I have been going about canvassing now, until I think everybody in Warrington knows ine. I have been canvassing with geatlemen who have spent their lives in Warrington, some of them bred and born here, some of them having spent 40 years of their life here, and as I go along the strePPa they say to me, " Why, you know more people than we do." In going about the streets 1 know the short cuts better than many of the Waitiugton people ; and yet they tell me lam a stranger. Well, I have been a stranger, but I think lam a stranger no longer. (Applause.) Now Orr chairman has told us to get out of this ball in a very few minutes, so I will not detain you. I know that your interest is cestred in the result which will be an- nounced next Tuesday night. You are 311 wondering what it will be. I will tell you. We are going to win. (Loud cheers.) All yesterday the other side were going about say- ing that they were going to win by a great majority, but to-day they will tell yo ft that they think perhaps they will win, but they are not quite sure. (Laughter.) Now, gentle- men, this result has been brought about by the energy and the exertions of you who have been supporting the Liberal candidate in this contest. I thaiik you all for the work you, have done. I thank the ladies, as I said before, for what- they have done; and I think I know what the result is going to be from a little circumstance. When I go canvassing, the little children are all singing the Liberal songs that you have been singing in this ball. I have spoken about the ladies, and I have spoken about one lady friend we have in the gallery, and next to that one the most enthusiastic sup- porter in this meeting is a little child here, who has been waving his handkerchief all the time. He is on our aide. When we have the women, we are sure of the fathers. When we have the children on the Radical side, we are sure that England in the future is going to be Radical. (Loud cheers.) Now I know that I have much to thank you for, for the work that you have done during the last few weeks, and I kaow that a very severe tax will be put upon your loyalty to Liberalism owing to the polling day being fixed for Tuesday next. Alderman' Pickmere said the other day that the fixing of Tuesday bad been an advantage to the Tories, because it was a bad day, and because we were ios. ing four days which we could have got to Friday to increase oar majority. I know that the tax is going to be great upon you, and under the present Act, the Corrupt Practices Act, it is greater than it has been in the post. We shalt be allowed to have no conveyances, and those of our friends who are ill in bed and cannot get to the poll will have to be carried somehow. There will be no wheels to take them on. (A voice: "We can wheel them in a barrow." Laughter and loud cheers.) Our friend says you will fetch them in a barrow. When you bring them all in a barrow we shall l have won the borough. (Cheers.) 1• Mr. Dram then proposed :—" That the best thanks of this meeting be given to Mr. Percy for his excellent ad- dress, and to Mr. Stirrup for presiding over the meeting." The resolution as seconded and carried by acclama- tion. _ . _
The CHAIRMAN briefly returned thanks, sand the proceed- ings terminated.

Ha WILL MARRY MISS SALLY TODGERS.—" WYE is ze plaze for ze what-you-call-ern for ze marriage ?" inquired a Frenchman yesterday of the gentleman in charge of the marriage license department of the Orphan's Court. "11 faut zat las paper get for marry Sall." "Here you are," returned the Marriage Clerk, in his business way. "What is ,your name and age?" The Frenchman, evidently a sailor, answered all the necessary questions till the query was put as to the lady's name. " Sall " was all he knew. Well," said the clerk, "is that, all her name ?" " Mais sere ees plenty name enough. Sall ees right. Sally toujours. That's all." " Ah, yes." ex- claimed the clerk, with a sigh of satisfaction, "Sall Todgers. How old is Miss Todgers ?" " Twenty-seex." "hat day was she born ?" " Mais Ido not know. She do not know; zero is nobody zat know." "Was she ever married before ?" "Om, vunce ; it is five year." "Whore is her husband ?" "I do not know, 'e ees four year dead." "Did you know him ?" "Non, I was not acquent. Sacre, ees it necessaire zat I should him know? I do not like ze idee." It was explained that an ac- quaintance with the deceased was not absolutely essen- tial, though frequently useful, and the Frenchman paid his fifty cents and left the office with ate license to seek Sally Todgers, as the name appeared on the paper.— Philadelphia Press. Han MAJESTY'S STATE BROCCIL—The Koh-i-Noor—the magnificent diamond which our Queen so frequently wears as a brooch on State occasions—has a romantic history. Its name signifies "Mountain of Light" in the Hindostanee language. According to Hindoo legend, it was discovered in one of the mines of Southern India, and was worn by Kama, King of Agra, in the wars which terminated 3001 a.c., and which form the subject of the great epic poem of the East. Subsequently the unparalleled jewel became the property of the Sultans of Delhi, and was seen at that Court in 1665 by M. Tirvernier, a French traveller. From the Mogul Em- perors it passed to Nadir Shah, who headed the success- ful Persian invasion; subsequently it was taken by the ruler of Cabul, from whose successor, in 1813, Runjeet Sing, partly by threats and partly by a bribe of 25,000 rupees (about £12,000) obtained the famous diamond. When England annexed the Punjaub, the treasury of Lahore was confiscated to defray the expenses of the war, and it was stipulated that the Koh-i-Noor should be presented to the Queen of England. It was brought to England in the summer of 1850, in charge of Colonel Makeson and Captain Ramsay, and on the 3rd of July the chairman and directors of ' the Indian Board pre- sented it to her Majesty. It weighs 186 carats, and, valued on the ordinary scale, is worth about £270,000. Public Analysts have submitted CADBURY'S COCOA to close tests, and the result has always proved its great value as a sus- taining and nourishing beverage. Bewarora Imitations.— Advt.

RUGBY RULES. .. RUNCORN lizensaerfosi v. lLaw ,BEIGRTOx Ourram.— Played at New Brightou,on, Saturdarlast, the home team being well represented. The Recreation won by 1 try and (minor points to New Brighton nil. t Re:lcons V. ECCLES (SECOND TEAMS) —This match was Pfeyed at Runcorn, on &tut day. Runcorn were declared the victors by one goal two minor points to Eccles one minor Point. The game was well contested throughout, both teams playing a good game. hT. HELENS V. BLACECEY.—PIayed on the ground of the termer on Saturday and a fast game resulted in a draw, slightly in favour of St. Helens, who had had the best of the play throughout the game. SL Helens scored one try and five minor points to Blackley one try and one minor Point. Sr, BEMIS RECREATION V. NEWTON-LE•WALOWS.-- , Played ON the ground of the latter ON Saturday. The Re- ceeation played one short while Newton played a full team A. drawn game resulted, .the, Recreation scoring five minor. Points to one. Pyke, for the visitors, crossed the line, but the home team captain disptited the try. RUNCORN V. ECCLES.--PlNyed at Eccles, on Saturday, When a game of sixty minutes' duration ended in favour of Runcorn by one try two touchdowns to one dead ball. Johnson, who played a capital back game, secured oue try . from a pass by Speakman; the latter played a grand game, putting in some excellent runs, getting on several oc- easions on the verge of his opponents' lines. . WantanoTorr ("A") V. TRANDIERE.—The return match between the above teams was played at Tranmere on Settle- *. Tranmere kicked off and the first scrimmage was for- toed in neutral territory. On the ball coming loose Whittle transferred it to Bibby who, on attempting to run, was col- lated and losing possession let up the home forward, who _1 kicked over the line and forced Hewitt to touchdown. Hewitt • tltopped out and Blundell gaining possession ran strongly ' to the visitors' line, where he was tackled by Appleton, who had to retire. Bashford taking his place weakened Warring- ton in the forward division. Some tight scrimmages now took place in the visitors' 25, when Leitch, Nevins, and Whittle relieved by a good dribble WO the visitors quer- Leers, but Blundell soon ran the ball back to neutral ground, r torn a scrimmage in the home 25 Whittle passed to Bash- ford, who transferred to Bibby, the latter getting in but the point was not allowed. Walsh next got possession, Passed to Appleton, and this player taking his drop at goal torced Whyte to touchdown. From the kick-out play raged a,t Centre, when from a scrimmage the Warrington forwards prose away and dribbled the ball over, Jones completing the try close to touch. Walsh failed to register the major. Warrington Shortly after half-time was called the score being, warrington 1. try and 1 touchdown to Tranmere 1 touch- (l, own. On resuming Whittle kicked off, the. oall being returned to tootle- • where a scrimmage took place, Warrington gradaaily •removing play to the. ' home line when Tranmere by a combined dribble took the ball to centre. Warrington forced their way back, and from a scrimmage iv the home 25 Whittle obtained •poesession. and passing to Bibby, who on being Collared iransferredto ilashford, the latter succeeded in dropping a splendid goal. OR kickine off Fulton got hold and ran into the visitors' 25. Several scrimmages took place, from one of which Fulton Picked up, and. running strongly was knocked into touch Within a yard of the visitors' line. Play was now in the visitors' 25, bntehe ball was gradually forced ham and 'Warrington' rushed it over, forcing .Tranmere to touch down. Shortly after, time was called leaving Warrington victorious 1)1,1 golf, 1 try, and 2 minors to 1 minor. The . Warrington forwards played well to a man, the most notice- able being Molyneeux, Dillon, and Foster, whilst of the hacks Hewitt, Baal:ford, and Whittle were the best. War- rington team :—Full back, Hewitt; three-quarter backs, H. Boardman, Wppieron, and Bibby; half-backs, Whittle (cap- tain), and Walsh; ,for Warde Dillon, Molyneaux' Leitch %%ins, Liihman •Bashford, J. Jones, Foster, and tine.: Irorth, .

v°tlgh on Saturday. The game, which was very fast, teaulted in a draw, one goal each being scored. LINACRE V. PRESCOT (2ND TEAMS).—Played at Prescot eQ Saturday, before a numerous concourse of spectators, and a kindly-contested game resulted in a victory for the Linacre by four goals to nil. ' liavrrorr CMIMON RANGERS (2ND; V. HAYDOCK RAM:GAMS IST).—Played on the ground of the former' and a very Pleasant game ended in an easy victory for the Rangers by three goals and two disallowed to none. LINACRE V. PRESCOT.—Tbie march was played on the ground of the former, at North-p.irk, Liverpool, on Satur- day, an' a pleasant galls r.sulted in a victory for the Linacre by three goals to nil. The visitors' backs defended finely.; whilst for Linacre A. Allsopp, T. Holmes, and W. Eturnphreys played beet. STOCKTON Hi3ATH V. SANKEY REFINERS.—A match be- tween the above took place on Saturday, on the ground of the former, and after a very pleasant game resulted in a draw, one goal each, Westbrook scoring for the home team, the goal for the Refiners being thrown in from touch and 'banded through by the home goal-keeper. • •

, . Niwrow UOMMON RANGERS (IST) V. RAVDOCK ST. ~,411V.5.S (2ND).—Played at Haydock on Saturday, when the t'a: was very even throughout. Harrison scored the first 0341 for the Saints, but Hell shortly afterwards equalised ' Matters, and Rigby notched a second point. On changing ends the game was well contested, Woreley being the first to score for the visitors, but the point was disallowed on the groond of off-side play. Soon afterwards Mather scored for the Saints, but the Rangers retaliated, and when time was celled the score was, Rangers, three goals and one disputed ; Nt. James, three goals.

Sorts, &swanla.—The soldiers ant cbmpletelv exhausted by five Bays of almost -continuous ;marching and fighting. At night they have nothing to cheer them except a ration ablaut bread for supper Mid tbecold muddy fields on which to blionack. .TlFit•Lte StifDia.—Yesterday evening a demonstration by Bulgarian studente took place in Vienna. Hundreds of them marched through the streets singing national SOMIS and praises of their Prince. They start for the seat of war to-n ght. Their telegram offering their services was an- swered by the Prince himself, who thanked them, but said be would not expose them to danger unless urgent neces- sity arose. This message raised their enthusiasm to the highest pitch, and they will not hear of staying behind. BELGRADE, SIINDAY.—The wounded continue to pour in- to Belgrade. Thirty railway carriages full arrived to-day. The wounded,wBfir-filisttremoved from the carriages and placed on straii"Mittritastis to rest, being afterwards con- veyed to the hospital in Carriages requisitioned for the pur- pose. The town is now so full that all the public build- ings have been reqiiisitioned for their accommodation. Sone, Susinay.A sanguinary engagement was fought this afternoon between the Servian and Bulgarian forces at Diagerntin. Tho latter' succeeded in driving back the See. vians from all the heights above the Dragoman Pass, and pow hold all the positions. The Bulgarian troops die- played the greatest bravery during the battle, Intelligence -from Widdin states that the town is surrounded by the Seri minas. An engagement was fought toklay in the but without any decisive result. "SOr.a., MONDAY.-1 despatch states that Widdin has been bombarded by the •Servians, and is in flames. BELGRADE, MONDAY.—The following is the view of the polities' situation held and sustained in official circles here: —The Bulgarians, it is argued, violated the frontier aiitl attacked the Servians on Servian territory at Vlassina.• King Milan thereupon declared war, and the Servians became possessors by right of conquest of a pz,rtion of Bulgarian territory. ' This wgs before Prince Alexander agreed to withdraw from Eastern Roumelia, and even should the King be bound by the note of his Government to the Powers de- manding a restoration of status quo ante, he would still, it is contended, have a right to the territory conquered prior to the Prince of Bulgaria acquiescing in the re-establishment of the status quo. Further, the question is asked, "Would the Powers decide on armed intervention either by one Power or conjointly, in .the event of the :Servians being able to hold the said territory?" • ' SEVERE DEFEATS AND. RETREAT OF THE SERVIANS. •

SOFIA, Mei/max.—Fighting took place on .Sunday in the Dragoman Pass... A Bulgarian infantry regiment, two dronjinesr a:battery of artillery, and a squadron of horse ar- tillery were despatched on a reconnaissance. Towards noon the cavalry perceived the enemy posted on the heights to the west of the pass. Meanwhile the Servian troops occu- pied a position -to the South of the Dragoman Pass, and a detached forte engaged the new corners until the arrival of the leftwing',Of the Bulgarian Army, when the first ridge 'was carrierkby' assault; thh Bulgailani reserving tiish; tire. eonsioning its advance, the 'Billgarfan'left ling' (4014 the enemy from ridge to ridge, while the right wingtnet with similar success. At six o'clock the Servians withdrew in disorder. The Bulgarians c.aptured )100 prisoners and One gun. BELGRADE, TrESDAY.—The SerViarill are retreating with- out fiAting, towards the frontier. The Bulgarians have occupied all the Servian positions and are advancing moon the frontier. The Servian headquarters hays been again mithdrasvn to Pirot. The second batch of Servian infantry, consisting-of fouribattalions, will leave to-day for the seat of war.and,will e.fellowed by the cavalry to-morrow, and r.tha artillery. on Thursday. It is statedtbat King Milon has resolved to bead a final attack ggainet the Bulgarians. The "fitlfureiroTaineral..Tayanovitelf and Col. Meskovitch have productil..great exasperation. Soria, Wittorrnsnair.—,-The King of Servia has sent a flag of truce to thi Bulgarian headquarters making a pro- posal for peace at the request of the great powers. The Bulgarian commander, by order of Prince Alexander, de- clined the proposal, the Bulgarian Government not having received any such communication from representatives of Oa powers, the Prince will not conclude peace until the Servians have evacuated Bulgarian territory in the Widdin district, and until the amount of the war indemnity to be paid by Servia should have been fixed. BELGRADE, WEDNESDAY.—At a conference of the repre- sentatives of the Powers held last evening in Belgrade, it was resolved to make, a collzctive proposal for the immedi- ate suspension of hostilities. BUCHAREST, MONDAY —The cannonade around Widdin lasted All night. At six o'clock this morning a large Ser- vian force, coming from Smardan and Tatargik, attempted an attack, but were repulsed after an engagement lasting three hours. CONCENTRATION OF AUSTRIAN TROOPS IN • HERZEGOVINA. Curren°, TUESDAY.—The news of a concentration of Austrian troops in Herzegovina is confirmed, and intelli- gence has now been received that three infantry regiments, one from Upper Austria, one from Lower Austria, and a third from Hungary, have proceeded via Slavonia to Bos- nia, where they are to be employed in forming a military cordon.

CESSATION OF HOSTILITIES. , SOFIA, WEDNESDAY MIDNIGIIi. No further fighting took place at Tsaribrod to-day, the Servian army is com- pletely demoralised. Large numbers of eryian prisoners have been brought here. DARMSTADT, TEDIUSDAY.—PfiIICO Alexander of Batten- berg to-day received the following despatch from his son, the Prince of Bulgaria Taaribrod, Thursday. 9-30 a.m. —We crossed the frontier to-day and, are going to Pirot. As fat as Widdin, Bulgaria is cleared of the Servians. Both of us are well." THE DIPLOMATIC SITUATION.

. Lord Salisbury arrived at the Foreign Office on Thurs- day afternoon front Hatfield, and, at four o'clock he was waited upon by the Russian. German, Austrian, and Turk- ish Ambassadors, who each had separate interviews with his lordship. It is understood that the subject of the inter- view referred to the . situation in Bulgaria and Servia, and the prevalent opinion is that the Powers will arrive at an understanding upon a joint Note to be despatched to Prince Alexander. HE BURMESE CAMPIIGN.—MORE THAN FORPY GUNS CAPTURED. ; Rarrooos, SITSDAY.—King Theebaw has issued another proclamation, in much the same terms as the former one. It conalu'deibLy Ordering 25,000 troops to held themselves in esadiness, and adds that an auspicious day has been selected fpr marching to seize Talaing Arakan and Tavoy, under the !Worship of the King himself. YKISANatAtriPO SUNDAY.—It is reported that 3.000 Bur- limns hreon their way down from Mandalay. We have been Otte unmolested. Two companies of Europeans and six nompaniea of Sepoys garrison the forts. Minhla has been strengthened. The flotilla Is here. The wounded offic'ers are doing well. There are many wounded Humans in the hospital. The strictest orders have been issued against in- terfering with the villages. The people are returning to their houses. More than forty guns have been captured since we crossed the frontier. The where- abouts of the Italians, who are conducting the river defence, is not known, We have received no news from Mandalay'. The fate of the Europeans there is doubtful.—Daily News,

THE CAPTURE OF MINHLA. . Mieart.,A, Nov. 17 (vra THEYETNYO) MONDAY. The !opts on both sides of the Irrawaddy at Minhla were taken hce storm today. Parties were landed simultaneously at patanago.on the left bank, and on the opposite bank a little iove Malohn. The troops on the right bank were the 2nd ueen's own Bengal Native Infantry, the 11th Bengal ative Infantry, and the 12th Madras Native Infantry, Wider the command of Colonel Harris, of the 11th, and colonel Baker, of the Queen's Owu. Difficulties comrnen- aid Om the very moment of lauding. The jungle, though lbw, was hicionceivably dense, so much so that the advance could Conlibe made along the narrow country lanes. Be- hind the cactus hedge* which lined these lanes the Bur- mese had concealed themselves, and fired upon us from all sorts of unexpected places. The closeness of thicket growth and the difficulty of hewing a way through rendered the work of dislodging them, and even of returning their fire, no easy task. This, however, was steadily done, and at last a stockade about a mile west of the town of Minduhla was reached. In itself it was too hastily constructed to be strong, but the surrounding jungle, swarming as it was with the King's troops, made the approach a matter of extreme difficulty. It nevi stubbornly held, and tbe Burmese kept up a sustained musketry fire, aided by a few light field. pieces. The stockade was attacked from two sides. Col. Harris led the assault on the left or river front; Lieutenant Downs, adjutant of the 11th, that en the right. On the left Lieutenant Drury, temporarily attached to the 11th, was mortally wounded while leading his company. ,The command was then taken by Maier Hill and Captain Peile. The stockade having been caiftured by a rush, the Gover- nor's palace, immediately beyond it, was then taken and burnt. The troops thereupon wheeled to the right and advanced eastward on the town of Minhla. The country was still thickly covered with jungle, l•at enough could 'be seen to direct the march On a high masonry building, which mounted 11 guns, several of them rifted, besides a number of cut. verinee. The Government river steamer Irrawaddy and the armed launch, the Kathleen, had for some time been ellen- ing this position, but withoat !Bitch succees in silencing the Burmese fire. Our troops on shore bad some severe fighting in the jungle to the north and east of the town be- fore they ateived within striking distance. The thickness of the cover. bad separated the men, and when the assault was made it was !)yot dozen men of different regiments. The Burmese waited for the attack., which had to be de- livered up a long ramp. The party was gallantly led by Lieut. Downes and Lieut. Wilkinson. The latter woe dangerously wounded by a slash on the head from a sword. The first handful of attackers were backed up by another pparty, h ue nci e resistance Major ie Hwatsl 18.1 igAtiftt s r Thet h e Captureenemy e this fled f in uast all d i centralr.c. tinns, and was vigorously followed up, acid many were shot down. A great part of the town was burnt, as well as the Governor's residence. The shells from the river fired a few houses, and the conflartra.tion rapidly spread among the flimsy bamboo huts. Major McNeil, of the Staff, was wounded early in the day, and having n.eyerthelese con- tinued to advance was hit again at the taking of the stock- ade. llie Injuries, however, are slight.
