FRANCE. Aling, WEDNESIDAY.—The newspapers to-day entant. mously recognise the gravity of the situation created by the election of a Committee of the Chambers favouring the evacuation of Tonquin, and anticipate a Ministerial crisis. DEATH OF THE KING ,OF SPAIN. . The Press Association learns that a telegram was receivq at the Foreign Office in London, on Wednesday, announc- ing the death of King Alfonso 111., which took place,at nine o'clock on Wednesday morning The cause of death is stated to have been consumption, accelerated by dysentery. The young Queen is reported to be quite prostrated by her bereavement. The Press Association states that during Tuesday night King Alfonso sank rapidly. Telegrams announcing the changes were received at the Spaeish Legation in London. It was known there at a late hour on Tuesday that His Majesty's life wee rapidly ebbing away, so that news of his death, which was received shortly' after noon en Wednesday, did sot cause much surprise. The Queen of England Was the first to announce to tbe Spanish Ambaseador in London the demise of his sovereign, and this she did by means of sympatheitc telegram addressed to the widowed Queen lf Spain. From the latest telegrams received at the Spanish Lega- tion, it is understood that the Queen was in claim attehd- mace upon 'King Alfonso at the time of his death. His Majesty, a few days ago, moved from the royal palace in Madrid to his beautiful seat at Pardo, near the capital, and it was here that he died. . In the Course of a brief conversation a representative* the Prise Association had with the Spanish ambassador, hiel excellency denied that there was any possibility of the present dynasty of Spain being disturbed by King Alfonso's death. The Princess of Asturias, the eldest daughter of the deceased monarch, now b,comes sovereign of the Spanish dominions. She, however, is only five •ears old, and there is no reason to doubt that her mother will be made Queen Regent, and that she will act in that capacity during the minority of her daughter. MADRID, WMDNESDA.Y. 6-15 P.M.—An extraordinary supplement to the Official Gazette was issued this afternoon announcing the death of King Alfonso at El Parade at a quarter to nine this morning, and adding that the President of the Council and other Ministers who were present in- formed Queen Christine, who becomes Regent according to the Coastitution, that their Mmisterial duties had termina- ted, ,and that they therefore respectfully teadered their •resignation. The Queen rt quested the Ministers to continue in offie• until she could attend to public affairs with more tranquility of mind. AMERICA.--eTERRIFIC.STORM ON THE NORTH- EASTERN COAST.

DEATH OF. THE VICE-PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES.. • NEW YORK, WEDSRBDAY EVENING.—Mr. . Hendricks died at Indianopolis. after attending the reception last night. He complained of pains in his side and stomach, and an they had not subsided this morning a physician was sum- moned, who administered an emetic and an injectien. The deceased remained in his room all day, keeping his bed for the greater part of the time. He died about five p.m., while Mrs. Hendricks was receiving visitors, no one being present at the time. His face gave no indications of pain of suffering. The cause of death Was paralysis of the heart.

COLONEL MeCORQUODALE AND NEWTON DIVISION. , The following letter signed "One .who knows appeared on Thursday in the liverpobl Daily Post • bir,—l was much, gratified on reading your note with regard to the coming election in this division, which ap- peared in last Friday's issue. No doubt all eyes are turned to this division, and tbe Liberals have been fortunate in :minoring such a worthy and exemplary candidate as Col. McOnrquodale. Your etateinents are true and indisputable, but there are several good points which reflect lasting credit on the Liberal ceiclidate, particularly as an employer of labour, which, at a time like the present, when many good. Intentioned voters May be in doubt which side to go for, should be remembered."

"Going back to 1847, we find Mr. McCerquodale arranging for his workpeople to work fifty-eight hours instead of sixty to the week; in 1865 4 denotation wtited upon him with a memorial for the hours to be reduced from fifty-eight to fifty-five per week, and this request was very courteously granted also. About twelve years ago he asked for repre- sentatives from each department of his works to meet him. On that occasion he said that he was pleased to state that trade was vory good, and he thought that in prosperous times it was the 6 unbounden duty of employers to remetn- ber their employed,' and be at once, quite unsolicited, gave an advance throughout the estab6shment, every journey- man receiving an addition of two shillings per week. Similar thoughtful actions are not unknown at the London, tiverpool, Leeds, Glasgow, and other works of his. . .

, "Now, about 1850 01 851. he gave the first of several soirees and balls in the old Conservative Hall (which was then for the first time lighted with gas). It was a splen- did affair, and in addition to all his workpeople being sumptuously provided for the sup.,riutendents of the Lon- 'don and North-Western and other railways, with the gentry of the surrounding districts, were present. "In religious matters and good objects he has always been to the front, and has ably discharged on several occa- sions since 1850 the duties of churchwarden at St. Peter's Church, Newton-le-Willows, to which aburch he is a liberal subscriber, and a few vears ago presented a fine organ at a cost of over £6OO. He is a regular communi- cant, and takes an active interest in its day and Sunday schools,

"lie is the executive chairman of the Haydock Explo- sion Relief Fund, and soon after _the sad exolosion at the Wood Pit he and his family organised an excellent bazaar in the Newton Town Hall, with a view of giving something extra at Christmas time to the widows and chi:dren. The bazaar realised'between £9OO and £300; and for three years in anccession about eighty widows received half-a. sovereign each extra, and over 200 children received five shillings each extra, which truly gladdened their hearts at a time of Peace on earth and goodwill to man.'" "Colonel McCornuodale is eloved by his workpeople ; there are scores in the Newton -establishment alone who have been with him over twenty-five years, and there area lot of others who have been with him front twenty-aye to tbirty.mine years. Throughout his practical business career he has set a noble example. His appintment as High Sheriff of this county was a befitting and graceful act of the country in acknowledgment of his sterling worth, and a man of such moral grandeur is in every way worthy of sitting in the honourable position as member of Parliament for this important division of the county."

div.head: CANDIDATURE OF SIR R. CROSS.
div.p: THE CANDIDATURE OF SIR R. CROSS.

STUBSHAW CROSS. On Saturday afternoon tha Home Secretary addressed a meeting of Conservative electors in the Church schools at Stubshaw Cross+, in furtherance of his candidature for the Newton Division. Mr. E. J. Crepper preelsed, and was supported on the platform by Lord Gerard the Hon. W. Gerard, Colonel Blundell (Conservative candidate for Inc.), Captain &ton, Messrs. John Steals, Marcus Brown-West- head, D. Grimke, 0. Wa'matey, W. H. Arnott, John Pear- son, T. Pearson, J. Pickering, T. Heald, &c.—Sir RICHARD Caoss remarked that the electors had now to decide some great issues with reference to the Government of the coun- try for the future, and they must not suppose that the pre- sent election was like others which had preceded it, at which no vital principle was involved. lie commented upon proposed reforms and the Free Education question and in alluding to the late Cmservative Government said that when they had been able to accomplish so much in a few short months the electors ought to hesitate before they turned them out. (Hear, hear.) A series of questions had been addressed to him by the mem- bers if the Farmers' Club, end he certainly thought he had I been the farmers' friend, and he believed they would find that the Conservative party were the same. (Cheers.)—Mr.C. F. Clarke moved, and Mr. J. Pickering seconded, a naotioe in favour of the Tory candidate.—Colonel Blundell and the Hon.W. Gerard supported the resolntion,which was carried ; though a considerable number of bands were held up to the contrary. BOLD On Saturday evening Sir Richard Cross addressed a crowded meeting of his supporters in the National Schools, Bold. The chair was occupied by Mr. W. Tipping, of Held Hall. Sir Richard Cross deplored the destructive attack which was made upon the House of Lords by the late Government, and said the people were imiebted very much to the gentlemen cons posing that assembly for many of the blessings which they at pre,ent enjoyed, not the least among which was the present Franchise Bill It the Estab- lished Church were destroyed and despoiled of her posses- sion!, and rendered less powerful for good, the immediate results would be the propagation of Socialism and atheism in this country. (Hear, hear.) They knew what atheism had done in France, and he would advise them to keep it away from these shores. (Hear, hear.) At present the Established Church of this country formed a regular wall against atheism and s-)cialism. (Cheers )—A vote in favour of his candidature was carried. EARLESTOWN. •

A meeting of the supporters of Sir Richard Cross was held in the Viaduct Institute, Etrlestown, on Wednesday night. Mr M Brown Westhead presided,and there were on the plat- form Lord Gerard, Colonel J Irelind•Blazkburne. Captain Seto°, and Messrs Thomas and Robert Stone, W F Gooch, J.P., B Glover R Houghton, JP, A L Evans, 0 Clarke, R H Wright, H. Monk, and others.—Colonel J Ireland-Blackburne, the retiring member for South-West Lanpashire, said it bad been his wish to do his utmost to promote the interests of the constituency. Sir Richard Cross addressed the meeting' at considerable length. Ha said the time of agitation was over, and the time of action was at band, and if he was to believe what be was told the Lancashire men had made up their minds about the vote on Monday next, and if they voted as they ought to do, he had no doubt they would vote for himself, and uphold that Constitution under which they had had 80 much happiness and so many blessino (Applause.) He commented on the result of the elections on the preceding day, and following with a reference to obstruction in the House of Commons. Speaking on the land question, he said he was in favour of having small allotments to every cottage throughout the country. He asked them to return the Conservatives to power, • (Applause.)—Mr. Alfred Turner proposed, and Mr. William Carson seconded, a reso- lution of confidence in Sir Richard Cross, which, after being supported by Mr. Bircb3,ll and Mr. Pierpoint, was carried.

PROPOSAL TO TAX CORN.—Mr. James Lowther, who is prosecuting a vigorous Canvass in the Louth Division of Lincolnshire, informed a meeting at South Kelsey that if he were placed in the position of a responsible Minister with a good majority at his back, hi would certiinly bring in a measure to put a duty on corn. Mn. CHAMBERLAIN'S RELIGIOUS VlEWS.—Writing in reference to to a Tory statement that he was f' a Comtist, a hater of Christianity, and an atheist," Mr. Chamberlain says he is not and never has been a member of the Comtist Society; he has never spoken or written a word against Christianity; and he is a member of' the Unitarian body, and was for some years a Sunday school teacher in Bir- mingham. The right hon. gentleman doer not think the cause of religion gains much by the misrepresentations which are made concerning him. POLITICAL CANDIDATES AND THE TEMPERANCE QUES• norr.—The Parliament try Committee of the Licensed Vic- tuallers of the United Kingdom has issued a stttement showing the attitude of the candidates now before the Eng- lish constituencies on the subject of SinVay clueing and Local Option. Thu figures put forward ehow.that 233 cin- didates are in favour of Sunday closing, and 240 against. 'while 519 have not given a decided opinion. On the Local Option question there are 247 for and 260 against a measure of this kind, while 437 five no veice. WHAT IT Is To BE A CONSERVATIVE—The following defi• nition of what it is to be a Conservative is from the Rea of a well-known novelist. It is to reverence the divinity of rust and corruption ; to rivet afresh the chains of tradition and of superstition ; to bind the free limhs of living men in the fetters of the past ; to turn blind the era from the light, and deny to thirsty lips the waters of truth ; to say to the crowned fool "You are God's elect," and to the poor I "You are beasts of burden, only not, like other beasts, I worthy shelter or fodder ; to cling to falsehood, and to I loathe reason.

-1-Itow :IN Conttrwatt.—A meeting of Mr. Pendarves *lrian's committees from various parts of the.North-Weet Division of Chfnwall was held on Monday. at'Camborne. A Mob aseembled, and hustled the various members as toey Arrived. I ['he rough horseplay gave place to stone throwing The windows of the Town Hall and adjoining hotel were emesbed. The president of the opposition committee and the other candidate himself earnestly appealed to the crowd to atop rioting and disperse, but in vain. Several of the obnoxious committee suffered severely. There were several iSolice present, but they were powerless to in- terfere. APOLOGY BY LORD RANDOLPH. CHURCHILL.—A. year ago, when rioting occurred at Aston Grounds, Birmingham, in connection with a Conservative demonstration, Lord ft. Churchill made some severe charges and accusations agaiest the Birmingham Corporation. Addressing the electors of the Central Division of Birmingham the other night, his lord- ship tendered a public apology for having made his random and unfeunded charges. He told his audience that if any expression he used could inflict personal pain upon any member of the Corporation, or could be considered in any way derogatory to their honour and ability to discharge public duties, those expressions be should be anxious to qualify and to withdraw and express regret for. DUCKING TORY OasraomoNtsrs.—On Saturday even- ing at Bekby, at a meeting in support of Mr. Ratcliff, Liberal opponent to Lord John Manners, owing to the Con- servatives having threatened to break up the gathering, several hundred Liberals with lighted torches marched in

procession some miles to a barn, the only place obtiinable for the meeting. When the proceedings commenced, a °numerative farmer pulled a brick out of the barn, and withlnhers disturbed the proceedings. Eventually acne Liberals sallied forth, and ducked both the farmer and an accomplice in an adjoining brook,completely sousing them, and one or two other persistent obstructionis's were roughly handled. Afterwards the meeting was uninterrupted. LORD HARTINGTON AT Reverzersratr., —Lord darting- ton, speaking at Rawteostall on Wednesday night, depre- cated the idea that the result of the elections should be judged by the few contests already decided, though be augured favourably for the Liberal cause from cases like Birmingham. He maintained tdat an absolute Liberal majority over the Conservatives and Parnell ites would en- able the Government to deal with Ireland in the spirit of justice and firmness. On the other hand, they accession of a weak Tory Government would mean a weak policy in Ireland, where the administration of the law would be governed by the retention of the suppnt of the Irish party. He also dis.cussed questions of local government and fair trade.

DISGRACEF7L SCENE AT A NOMINATION.—An extraordi- nary scene took place at the nominatien of candidates for Sheffield, oe Monday. Dr. Millar, who has been con- spicuous during the electioneering turmoil, moue his ap- pearance before the Mayor, accompanied by his election agent, Mr. Peasegood. The latter having banded in the nomination paper On behalf of Dr. Millar, the Mayor at once declared it invalid, whereupon the doctor, exclaiming fiercely," Get out of my eight," made an onslaught on Mr. Peasegood, battering the unfortunate agent about the bead with his hat. The Mayor, interposing, orckred Dr. Millar to desist, or he wemld send for the constables, and the doctor, thus admonished. left the room, followed after a discreet interval by Mr. Peasegood.

• Loan SALISBCRY ON GENERAL. TOPICS.—There was a large gathering of Metropolitan Conservative candidates at the house-dinner of the Sr. Stephen's Cl ub on Monday night. Lord Salisbury responding to the toast of the Couservative cause, warned his party against being led by the vapourtng language of their opponents into the belief that Conservatism had no hope. He believed the contest would be close, and they must work unceasingly, believing that no constitnency was certain and no constituency hopeless. Tee Liberal leaders had Striven bv lavish promises of home legislation to draw the electors' attention from their disastrous foreign policy, but be believed that the artifice had failed. Mr. Gladstone's utterances on the disestablishmt-nt of the Church had proved a grievous tactical bluntler, and nothing bad done more to hamper the right hon. gentleman in his Mid- lothian "pilgrimage." Lord Salisbury twitted the Liberal leaders, themselves divided on material points, with their frantic efforts to attain and preserve unity amongst ,their followers, and said he believed that the Liberal boasts of coming victory would prove utterly baseless. Tint FAIR TRADE DELUSION.—The Statist says :—There is a complete delusion on the part of Fair Traders as to the influence of foreign Protectionist measures upon our tra.le Various of our industries may he depressed by foreign com- petition, but that competition arises, not because of, but in spite of, the Protectionist measures of foreign Governments, and would continue to exist whether those Protectionist measures are continued or not. The Fair' Trader is equally under a delusion as to the possibility of remedying the pre- sent state of our trade or promoting its prosperity by means of retaliatory duties or duties imposed for the purposes of Protection. It has been easy for Liberals to prove that if we are to revive trade by putting duties upon foreign man- ufactures. that measure will certainly aggravate the evil. We import such a very small amount of manufactured artieles as compared with what we export, that in playing the game of imposing duties on such articles we could not possibly be successful. If we attempted it the only result would probably be that foreign Governments would increase their duties on our macufactures still more, and our last condition would be worse than the first.

LORD SALISBCRT ON DISESTARLISIIMENT.—In reply to an Edinburgh correspondent, who asked for an expression of his views an the Church question "as a guidance for those ' who place the interests of the Church above other and purely political considerations," Lord Salisbury has written a long letter dealing with the disestablishrnent proposals, and the utterances of Mr. Gladstone. He says Mr. Gh.cl• stone has avoided giving a direct opinion on the question as regards England, apparently in the hope of not offending a powerful section of his party. In regard to Scotland, he declined te support the proposal because it was not ripe for treatment in the next Parliament. The phrase implied that in due time it would be ripe, and would then be acted upon. The mass of Liberal candidates were pledged to the principle, and it was very doubtful whether Mr. Gladstone's influence could induce them to vote against the proposal, which would certainly be introduced. If Dr. Cameron's re- solution were carried, it would be a fatal blow to the Church Her opponents would be strengthened, and her de- I fenders would enter upon the final struggle with a sense of 'impending defeat. Lord Salisbury's advice, therefore, is Ithat support of the Church raust be made a test que•tinn above all others at the elections. -

STORRIN-G A TORY greitehkare.—A good story for dad vaesers and others was recently told to the Liberal candi- date for one of our Yorkshire sea-coast towns. He had , called to see one of his supporters, a steady, intelligent, and respectable working man, who has a wife as true to her principles as himself. A Tory lady and two Tory gentlemen had called one evening to canvass the voter. He told them at oace and firmly that he was a Liberal, and had promised to vote for the Liberal candidate. They , nevertheless did not hesitate to try to persuade him to break his word and to promise for the Conservative; and the working man and his wife had to bear the imper- tinence as well as they could. At last one of the " gen- tlemon " said that Mr. Giadstone was the greatest traitor in I England! "I could bear it no longer," said the wife to the Liberal candidate, "so I jumped up and pointed to a portrait (of Mr. Gladstone) hanging near the door. I said, 'Do you see that ? It is only in a wood frame; but, if I could afford, I would have it framed in gold Now, you have had your answer. There's the door!'" To which door she pointed so reselutely that the three can- VASSere took their departure ; perhaps having learned that it might be well in future to treat a working man and his wife with something of the courtesy they would themselves expect. THE limn VOTE.—Tne Home Rule manifesto to Irish- men is England and Scotland was issued on Saturday. It reviews the legislation of the last five years affecting Ire- land, and urges that in no case ought an Irish Nationalist to give a vote to a member of the Liberal or Radical party, , except in some few cases in which courageous fealty to the ' Irish cause in the last Parliament has given a guarantee that every pledge will not be broken in obedience to the call of the Whip and the mandate of the Caucus.—Address- ing a meeting of Irish Nationalists in Liverpool on Monday night, Mr. Parnell said that on going into the figures Closely he came to the conclusion that it would be absolu- tely impossible for him to carry the division, and he did not thetefore think it prudent to come forward to a certain defeat, and be the flrst memseer of the Irish party to be de- feated in the great struggle now going on. tie had there- fore withdrawn his nomination for tl+e Exchange Division, and in being compelled to take that course by tbe opposi- tion of the Tory candidate be thought he was not bring well treated. The Executive of the National Irish League of Great Britain and Ireland have received numerous ap- plications from candidates requesting support at the poll. In the various constituencies for which they are candidates the Irish electors, by direction of the Executive, will vote for Messrs. Cowen, Storey, Thomsen, Labouchere, and Lloyd Jonee.—Jfichael Dav;tt De7l.92llWeS dir. Parnell.— Mr. Devitt publicly expressed regret on Sunday at the course recommended by Mr. Parnell to the Irish electors of Great Britain. The occasion was the annual demonstra- tion in Dublin in honour of the memory of the persons styled "The Manchester Martyrs." A Fenian procession marched to Glasnevin Cemetery, and two new monuments over recently deceased Fenians were unveiled, and a pane- gyric pronounced by Mr. Fitzgerald, who Was recently pro- posed in vain as a candidate at several Parnellite conven- tions. Mr. Fitzgerald abstained from saying anything on the subject, but when there were loud calls for a speech from Mr. Devitt, the latter took occasion to refer to the manifesto, and to the action oh the Tory Government. He said they were assembled to honour men who 15 years ago were struck down by the English Government because they endeavoured to free their native land. It was an encourag- ing sign that the sowardly and brutal Government whicu imbued its hands in the blood of Allan, Lakin, and O'Brien sat in Dublin that day, but dare not interfere with this demonstration ; but while they could proudly raise a shout of triumph over this Government, it was humiliating—at leaLt for him—to knew that Irish voters in England and Scotland who reverenced the memory of tcose men were now asked, for political reasons, to sapport teat brutal and cowardly and butchering Government.

RECAUSE there was a demand let such a medicine. 13ecausethere was a crying want for a remedy on which the peaple might depend in their hour of need, and "Gordon's Extract" has supplied that want, ant is Cling the aching void that existed before Pa advent. Bemuse " Gordon's Extract" enables the sick person be regain health, and the well one to keep it. •WARRINGTON, like many other Lancas.hite boroughs, has gone wrong; the Tory candy date was placed at the head of the poll OP Tuesday by a majority of 776 votes. This need si a large majority, and yet the Liberals nee, not despair • it is not more than five Pe:: cent of the electorate—a proportion which 4; by no means terrible in view of the ll° General Election, which, Mr. PARNELL is r, ported to have said, we may expect during t"," next twelve months. The causes of the dl5 aster which has overtaken so many Lanca. shire Parliamentary boroughs are not far t° seek. There can be no doubt that th „ef Church question has influenced a number A", electors—say one per cent. ; the Fair delusion may have undermined the allegian,:c. of another per cent. ; a third per cent. of defection may may be set down to misconcer tions on the Education Question; but tb;et. bulk of those who have transferred tb votes from the Liberal side to the side have done so at the bidding of PARNELL. The . Tory-Parnellite is a reality ; and its effects are pia': visible wherever the Irish vote constitoteili;• as it does in Warrington, a considel'ab4 proportion of the whole. Take the case Blackburn, which has a population vteif much similar to that of Warrington. st W. E. BRIGGS, Villo is unquestionably thell1;;t popular man in the borough, was returneu the head of the poll in 1880. Mr. CODDIrci TON, the Tory member, who was then heltins him, now heads the list of the four candidates with a majority over Mr. BRIGGS of no leS than 2,429, while Sir ROBERT PEEL, a str,taill: ger to the town, has a majority over BRIGGS of 1,686. The lush vote in ElaCnre burn, with a population of r tz,ooo, is 111 A, than double that of Warrington, and the verse majority, it will be noted, is more tut! r double. An analysis of the polling in ntue Lancashire towns would, we do not hesitatet to say, furnish a similar result. It is true thaa at St. Helens the Tory candidate has but it small majority; but he none the less owes to Parnellite dictation. Those who are hind the the scenes know that, if the Irish elec.: tors had not at the last moment broken their: Ipledges, Colonel GAMBLE would have beeve ! elected by such a majority as would the left the Tories almost hopeless for future. On the other hand, if we turn • iChester, where the followers of Mr. PARN.EAL are few, we find a Liberal returned, not" standing the fact that the two political partie are pretty equally divided. We are not arguing that so far as the boroughs are CO cerned there is no evidence of an uncer- tain mood, outside Irish and Catholic influences; there is undoubtedly a de-- fection. but that defection is small where the Irish vote is small. There is reason to hope, therefore, that the Liberal gains in the counties will make up the lassos' in the towns. The Tories have had matters ' pretty much their own way in the English counties ; but the views of the agricultural labourers have been wholly misapprehended if they do not vote Liberal on the first use they make of the franchise. The race is at present a neck-and-neck race between Liberals and Tories ; but the Liberals are likely to shoot a-head during the ensuing week. Whether they will get so far in
front as finish, PARNELL for ourse present
Office_ byl
would be the one h that they have cow, morality; have allic
1880, the of the Ir an unhol come to : good he. late, and come so' made of the vario try.
Whilst Franchise was in ar and the tants of the Newt especially Should be have forgo had had h vote tg gh the case, i have any s vote to helped the !talc* it ay in favour but the Ti

front as to be in a position, at the finish, to be independent ot Mr. PARNELL is a doubtful matter. Speaking for ourselves, we should not be sorry if the present Government were permitted to retain office by the grace of Mr. PARNELL. It would be such a cat-and-dog life as would on the one hand punish politicians who, in order that they may hold the reins of government, have committed the grossest political im- morality; and punish, on the other, men who have al-lied themselves with those who, in 1880, they denounced as the mortal enemies' of the Irish race. The alliance is, indeed, an unholy one; "it is not and it cannot come to good." Let local Liberals keep in good heart; their turn will come soon or late, and the probabilities are that it will come soon. Meantime the best must be made of the situation by helping to win in the various Divisions of this part of the coun- try.

THE polling for the Newton Division takes place on Monday, and, notwithstanding the adverse influence of Conservative successes in Warrington and St. Helens, the Liberals have strong hopes of returning Colonel MCCORQUODALE by a large majority. To begin with, the Division is less dependent on the Irish vote than many other constituencies in Lancashire, while as to the question of Disestablishment, Which Conservatives have insisted upon thrusting to the front, it is known that the Liberal candidate is as good
a Churchman as Sir RICHARD CROSS. In- deed, tested by his acts, he bears the palm, for not only is he known as a liberal subscri- ber to the St. Peter's Church, at Newton-le.

_ Willows, but his generosity went so far a few years ago as to cause him to present an organ at a cost of over £6OO. The Tories make a great mistake in seeking to identify the Es- tablished Church with the Conservative cause. They cannot afford to flout such Liberal Churchmen as Colonel MCCORQUODALE, for

_ .... _ _ thos n e who kow him well do not need to be told that he has from the first declared him- self as opposed to Disestablishment. This will be no recommendation to the Radical sec- tion; but Radicals are above all practical poli- ticians; they know that the Church question cannot be dealt with by the next Parliament,

and they will vote" for the Liberal candidate as one who adheres to the GLADSTONE pro- vamme pine and simple. Mr. GLADSTONE himself knows and acknowledges this; for in a letter which Mr. A. C. MCCORQUODALE received from the great, leader of the Liberal party no later than Thprsday last, he says : " I honestly desire the sgccess of Colonel MCCORQUODALE in the contest. in Newton Division of South-West Lancashire." Whilst there was a doubt as to file Franchise Bill passing, and the country was in arms against the Tory Opposition and the House of Lords, the inhabi- tants of the district now comprising the Newton Division showed themselves especially earnest in demanding that justice Should be done to them. Surely they cannot have forgotten that, if Sir RICHARD CROSS had had his way, they would have had no vote tg give on Monday next; and, this being thg Case, if they are true to themselves, and have any sense of gratitude, they will give the vote to the candidate of the party that helped them to obtain it. The Tories would tnakw it appear that they have always been in favour of an extension of the Franchise; but the House of Commons division list is lgainst them. Sir RICHARD CROSS was in Parliament from 1874 to 1879, when the Tories were in power, and, more than that, he was in the Ministry. What happened? Mr. TREVELYAN for six years in succession brought forward a resolution in favour of ex- tending the county franchise, and Sir RICHARD void against it in every division. le was in favour, too, of Flogging in the Army, for he voted on July 17th, 1879, against Lord HARTINGTON'S motion which condemned "the permanent retention of corporal punishment for military offences." lie was opposed also to Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S Bill for the extension of the hours of polling, so that so far as the working-men of Newton Divison are concerned they have a candidate in Sir RICHARD who has done all he could to prevent them having a vote, and sought to deny those who had a vote the opportunity of recording it without making a great sacrifice. Colonel MCCORQUODALE has not, however, been doing mischief. His record makes it clear that he has been just and kindly to his fellow- ken. He twice reduced the hours of labour of his work-people when memorials on the sub- ject were presented to him; and, twelve years ago, he showed the nobility of his character by advancing wages without being asked to do so. He was prosperous, and he desired that those who worked for him should prosper with him. The electors of Newton may trust their interests to a man of this kind; they are fortunate in having such a candidate, and if they do their duty they will be rewarded by having Col. MCCORQUODALE as their repre- sentative in the new Parliament. icre

THE Addresses of both candidates for the Northwich Division are now before the eleC- tors ; and, as both gentleman have spoken at length at a large number of meetingp, most of the new voters will by this have made up their Minds as to Whom they mean to support on Tuesday next. We have previously remarked On the sterling qualities of the Address which Mr. BRUNNER has placed before the public. There is none of that beating about the bush Which chhracterises the Address of Mr. VER- bni, the Tory candidate. Mr. BRUNNER uses language to express—not to conceal thought. Referring to the question of sub- sidence in the salt district which naturally ex- ercises the minds of the North wich electors, M I M. BRUNNER hits the nail on .the head by saying outright that the loss to owners p.aid tenants should be made good, and th " brine ought to be allowed to esc;po payment of its share of this loss." Mr. Vaßnlrr is uot as yet ready ":th remedy for :i any this crying evil:c, but he is willing to i -oquire intq the matter. He would relegatq tht question to a, Royal Com- '..".l.lssiort, that after spending a long tune tthd a latgt sum of money would produce a Rine Book which nobody would read and 'noboay act upon. Mr. BRUNNER demands in the way of Land Reform something more than cheaper transfer, and registering of titles, .as suggested by his opponent. He would go to the root of the meter by preventing the creation of life interests, thus leaving each Owner of land " a free man, free to sell, and free to let." Speakinc, on this subject in diriburgh, on Tuesday, Mr. GLADSTONE Said :--- fj have consulted legal authorities, and I tell you iuls, the reason why no man except a man with a Why the can as a rule touch land—the reason why the simplest operation cannot now be perfor- Illed as to land without calling for the aid of the ytraost resources of the legal profession, and impos-- 14g upon them heavy labours which necessarily must tutaa a certain remuneration—the reason why the

div.head: iiiiiimi._ J. -' \ , ,
div.p: iiiiiimi._ J. -' \ , ,

access to the possession is attended both with uncertainty, and with charge, and with long delays, is entirely to be found in one and the same thing, and that is in the existence of life estate or entail. (Cheers.) It is this that makes the business com- plicated, and the best legal opinions are to the effect that it is totally idle to talk of cheap and easy transfer of land and simple transactions with re- spect to land until you have abolished entail in life estate. That is one of the main objects that the Liberal party of to-day have in view. That is one of the purposes on which they are thoroughly and completely agreed. (Cheers.) Mr. BRUNNER would also abolish the un- just law of distraint; and put an end to the system whereby landlords are in a position to rob their tenants by attaching to themselves what is attached to the freehold. Both can- didates are in favour of licensing reform ; but the Tory candidate shows that he lacks faith in the people; he prejudges the issue by say- ing "a license should-not be refused renewal without adequate compensation." Mr. BRUN- NER does not fence himself in any way; he says simply and broadly that he is "pre- pared to give to the people in each locality full control of the liquor traffic" With regard to trade depression, the Liberal candidate truly remarks that the unlocking of the land will increase our harvests, the enfranchise- ment of leaseholds will stimulate the building trades, and in this way town and conntry will alike be largely benefited. The Tory candi- date, Tory-like, is willing to inquire ; he will leave the matter to the Royal Commission There are several other points of difference (including the reform of the House of Lords) regarding which Mr. BRUNNER is seen to great advantage as compared with Mr. VERDIN, who may be set down as one of ' those mongrel politicians who pass under the name of Liberal• Conservatives. Mr. BRUN- NER may be described as Radical, meaning by that "a Liberal who is in earnest ;" he is the right sort of man to send to the ne.w Parliament, for he means to go 'ahead and get something done. It is to be hoped that' the energy he has displayed will prove con- tagious, and that his supporters will work so as to secure a victory, on Tuesday, of which they and he may alike feel proud.

THE Campaign in the Widnes Division is being pushed forward vigorously on the part of the Liberals. • The polling takes place on Wednesday next, and, if intelligence, high character, and long service in the cause of the people count for anything amongst the new voters, Mr. MUSPRATT will be returned in spite of the efforts which are being made to mislead the Irish electors Speaking at Whiston, on Saturday, the Liberal candidate made short work of some of the nonsense talked by Mr. EDWARDS-MOSS. He showed ; indisputably that Free Trade had cheapened bread and other nccessaries of life; and, in reply to the atcusaiion that he did not know when the tax on sugar was abolished, Mr. MUSPRATT reminded his juvenile opponent that he formed one of a deputation fifteen years ago which was instrumental in inducing a Liberal Chancellor of the Exchequer to make a great reduction in the duty on sugar. He was desirous now of helping to abolish the imposts upon tea, coffee, and cocoa; and 1 of adjusting the burden of taxation all round I in such a way that the rich would be com- pelled to bear a just proportion. Mr. Mus= PRATT expressed himself in favourable terms as to the Miners' Programme, and as Mr. EDWARDS - MOSS, like his sponsor, Rh' RICHARD CROSS, gives forth a very uncertain sound on this subject, there is reason to believe that the miners will be sufficiently alive to their own interests to give a solid Liberal vote. At a meeting at Garston, on Monday. evening, Mr. Mus- pftArr dealt with the much-abused question of education. He emphasised the fact that he was in favour of abolishing school fees as a means to the spread of knowlege, and struck home when he said the Tories as a. party had I never been in favour of education. As an ad- vocate of equality, he would put Board Schools on the same footing as denomina- tional schools; and he pledged himself not to support any measure which would inter- fere with the freedom to give religious teach- ing in denominational schools. The hollow- ness of the Tory cry for local government was thoroughly exposed, Mr. MusPaArr carrying the war into the enemy's camp by reminding his hearers that when the Tories previously brought in a bill upon this subject thy-3r framed it in such a way that the members ot the governing Board would, if it had been adopted, have been comprised to he extent of two-thirds of the whole of justices of the pace. What was now re- quired was a ruling authority elected out-and- out by the ratepayers, and responsible to the ratepayers; and for a measure based on these sound principles they must look not to the Tory but to the Liberal party. Mr. MUSPRATT was not less effective in lav- ing bare the fallacies of Sir RICHARD CROSS on the land question, whilst he put to shame those who would seek to improve trade by adopting a restrictive tariff on manufactured goods. An overflow meeting, we should add, was held the same evening, and at both gatherings resolutions were passed pledging those present to use every legitimate means to secure the return of the Liberal candidate. We trust these pledges will not be in 'vain, that every Liberal will work as he has never worked before, and that the Widnes Division will help to swell the majority which is being given in support of Mr. GIADSTONE, the greatest statesman of the age, and "the noblest figure of the nine- teenth century."

Tun Ray. W. PRESTON, OF RUNCORN, ON DISESTABLISIP MENT.—At Trinity Church, Runcorn, en Sunday night, tliS Rev. Wm. Preston, MA., preached a special sermon on di.- establishment. He said an unholy effort was being made ' by men who professed to be Christians, and hy men who were Atheists, to separate religion from the State. He asked, if the Church were disestablished, would the sects rest satisfied with each other? No ; human nature was ever the same. Two hundred years ago the cry of to-day against the Church went up, and disestablishment came. They who brought it about soon established themselves in the place of the Church. They took possession of the vicarages and tithes. Among them was 'a notable Noncon- formist minister, the Rev. M. Serjeant, an ancestor of Mr. Chamberlain, who thrust himself into the vicarage of Stone, near Kidderminster. The prayer book was forbidden under Imprison:gent. The clergy were persecuted, until the na• don could endure it no longer, and the Church was restored to its lawful pomition as the National Church. The over- throw of the Church would be but the prelude to the over• throw nf the constitution and opening the door to the floods of Repttblicanism, Communism, and Socialism, and the ohief sufferers would be the working classes.—At the close of the service the anthem " God save the Queen " was sung by the whole congregation. BRIEF MARRIED HAPPINESS AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Annie Green, of 2, John- street, sumaioned Ann Green, her mother-in-law, for using false and defamatory language regarding her. From a statement made by Mr. Knowles, who appeared for the cona- plAnant. it appeared after a married life of nine weeks the defendant's son beat his wife, and at the end of twelve weeks left her through his mother's influence. On the 17th inet the defendant went to the complainant's house for the pawn ticket of her eon's watch, and then made serious charges against the girl's character. The couple. Mr. Knowlea stated, were little more than boy and girl.—After hearing a number of witnesses, the Bench bound the defen- dant over to keep the peace four months, herself in £5 and two sureties nf £5 each. _ _

A CITY VICAR AND Ills CURATE.—The city Press relates, with regret, in view of the cry of Disestab- lishment, the story of a city vicar who, with £1,500 a year, employed a curate, to whom he paid the magnificent stipend of £2O a year, to do the bulk of the work. But the curate desired an increase, and ventured to suggest in future he should be paid £25 per annum. The Vicar, however, was highly indig- nant, and forthwith dismissed his assistant. Much more in accordance with the Vicar's views was the reverend gentleman who next became his curate, for Ile offered his services for nothing, and the worthy 1 Vicar generously offered the use of his house—which, by the way, he did not want, as he was non-resident. The new-corner, however, being a married man with a family, and in want of money, suggested that he should have some small monetary .remuneration. "0," said the generous Vicar, "I will give you per- mieeion to take in lodgers !" A largely-attended meeting Hi furtherance of the Candidature of MI-. E. K. Muspratt for the Widnes Division was held on Saturday evening in the Na- tional Schools, Whiston. Mr. Alex. Eccles occupied the chair, and among those present were I'rofessor Sheldon (Liberal candidate for Ormskirk Division), the Rev. H. B. Williams (Wrexham), Messrs. Thos. Snape, E. S. Eccles G. H. Croxden Powell, G. S. Aldrich, E. Fidler, W. Tyrer, W. Mackenzie, H. B. Shores, J. A. Doughan, J. B. Leach, W. H. Leach, C. R. Aldrich, John Edwards, IL Edwards, A. P. JL Eccles, P. Edwards, Josiah Hayes, and W. Gerrard. Mr, MESrasft-r dorigtatttlated the people of Whiston ticrern now having an increased franchise pointing out that it was the Liberals, and not the Conservatives, who had given it to them. As to dizestabliehment, it was not now a question of prectical politics, and ought not to be dealt with until it was put before the country. He believed that the payment of school fees WAS a great im- pediment to the regularity of children attending school, and he should vote for the abolition of fees if by so doing it would not interfere with the management of denomina- tional schools; but he had shown them that this scheme for the abolition of fees could be carried out by the increased capitation grant, and would leave the management of denominational schools in ex- actly the same hands as they were at present. •Mr Edwards-Moss had said that free trade had decreased I the prices of the luxuries of the rich, but had not reduced the cost of the necessaries of life to the poor. Was there any men in that room whb would believe that statement? (••• No.") Why, free trade, if it gave us anything, gave us cheap corn. trappleuse ) He did not know that that was a luxury of the rich, but rather thought it was a necessity of the uoor. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Edwards-Moss had accused bins of not knowing that the tax on sugar WAS abolished. He would like them to tell Mr. Moss, when he cathe to ad- dress them at Whiston, that long before the tax on sugar was abolished, he (Mr. Muspratt) went as a deputation tea the Chancellor of the Exchequer (Mr. Lowe), 15 or 20 years ago, to ask for the abolition of that amongst other duties. and it was on the representation of that deputation that Mr. Lowe, when he breught in his budget, effected a great reduction in the duty on sugar. (Applause.) He would like them to go further, and remind Mr. Moss that Mr. Gladstone' Government, in 1874, had so managed the finances of the country that they had a surplus of six millions to be dealt with by their successors. Mr. Gladstone's Government had intended to abolish the tax upon sugar, which had been reduced before to a comparatively small basis, and would have done so had they been returned. (Applause.) He (Mr. Muspratt), if 'returned, intended to do all he could to obtain a readjustment of the taxation ef the country. so that it should net press so much as it did upon the poor. (Eleer, hear.) So far as he WAS concerned, what he desired in the case of tixstien was to abolish taxes upon tea, coffee, and cocoa. He considered the poorer classes too heavily taxed, and these duties were an impedi- ment to trade. He referred to the miners' programme which he bed received. To the qtrestion would he support Mr. Burt's amendment to the Employers' Liability Act, he replied that he was entirely in favour of Mr. Burt's bill, and would support it. With reference to the question would be support the Mines Regulation Act, so as to give the colliers checker men, he certainly would. With reference to the depression in trade, and especially agriculture, the great point was this—that the tenant had not security for any capital be invested in the soil. As to the royal commission on trade, they knew perfectly well what was causing depression of trade at the present time. He was in favour of a com- mission is inquire into the royalties in coal mines, with the view of getting rid of the royalties. They increased the cost of carriage, and it was disgraceful that foreign pro- ducts were carried cheaper than home products. Mr. P. Enwmans moved a resolution approving of Mr. Muspratt's candidature, and pledging the meeting to use every legitimate means to secure his return.—Mr. Shorreck Eccles seconded the resolution, which was sup- ported by the Rev. Mr. Williams, Mr. T. Snape, and P:o- -fessor Sheldon, and carried. MR. MUSPRATT AT GARSTOI.4. On Monday evening, a meeting in support of the candi- dature of Mr. E. K. Muspratt, the Liberal candidate for the Widnes Division, was held at the reading-room, Gars- (on, The room wan filled to its utmost capacity half an hour before the proceedings commenced. Mr. W. B. Bow- ring presided, and among those present were, besides the candidate, Messrs Holbrook Gaakell, J.P., F. H. Cio ssage, J.P., W. Oulton, S. K. Musprutt, James Handley, JP., Enoch Harvey, H. Brunner, H. Gaskell, jun., J. P. Gout- der, Craig, Smedley, Bebbington, J. M. M'Cullocb, and Carter, and the ReV. Mr. Cole. The CHAIRMAN, in his opening remarks, said Mr. Mae- pratt was a gentleman well known to them. He was a large employer of labour. He had a thorough knowledge of all the trades of their district, and he would, if elected to the House of Commons, be a representative, and an able repre- sentative, of all the requirements of the great trade carried OD in the Widnes Division of South-West Lancashire. That was a very great advantage in a candidate. He had been a persistent and pronounced reformer from his youth. His father was a reformer before him, and his was a soil In which grew no mushroom reforms. Mushrooms grew up rapidly in the night, and mushroom reforms grew up rapidly before ea election, but they died almost immedi- ately afterwards. (Cheers.) Mr. Moss, their opponent, gave a very long history to his supporters of his pedigree. What we wanted was the political principles of Mr. Moss. He told us that he had been seated at the feet of that Gam- . aliel of politics, Sir Richard Cross. (Groans.) We had no I experience of him as a politician, and we might be right in taking that he bad derived his political experience from that fountaM of political knowledge. If they were in ear- , neat in the great reforms of the immediate future we should I not look to Mr. Moss. If they wanted reform of our land laws-and he took it that all parties wanted reform of our land laws—(cheers)—if they wanted reform of our local govern- ment- (hear, hear)-if they might judge from the past, they would be seventy years in getting these things if they elected Mr. Moss. He would advise them to give their votes, not to Cross and Moss, hut to Mr. Muspratt and the " Grand Old Man." (Loud and prolonged cheering, after Which three cheers were given for Mr. eiladetotte). Mr. E. K. MIISPRATT, who was loudly cheered on rising, said before he went into those questions which he thought were most immediately before them, it was desirable he should say a few words upon two questions which had been raised by the Tories in order to call att eation away from the great reforms which the Liberal party had desired to pass in the immediate future to those which, if passed at all, would only be passed in the dim future. Many of the au- dience had heard, perhaps, what had been said by the Tories upon the question of education. The Tories—lie meant as a party, not individually—had never honestly been in favour of the education of the people. (Applause.) The Liberals

div.head: gERIOUS STABBING CASE AT RUNCORN,
div.p: gERIOUS STABBING CASE AT RUNCORN,

Before Mr. James Bandley, at Runcorn Police Court, yesterday, George Wilson was charged with unlawfully wounding John Wyatt. The men are sailors on board the schooner Agnes and Ellen, of Padatow, at present in Run- corn Docks and slept together in the lorecastle. Yesterday morning the mate called them to rise from bed for the pur- pose of commencing work as the vessel was to leave port by the afternoon's tide. Wyatt got up, and endeavoured to make Wilson rise also. He was shaking him a second time, when Wilson jumped up in a passion, some angry words passed, and then Wilson plunged his sheath knife into Wyatt's left breast, below the heart. A wound three inches long, and very deep was inflicted, and Dr. McDougall, who is attending the man, considers his condition highly dangerous.—The prisoner was remanded for a week. The annual meeting of this institution and the distribu- tion of prizes took place on Thursday evening. About 1,200 children front the various schools in the town occu- pied the gallery of the Drill Hall, and during the evening sang several part-songs in a capital manner under the leadership of Mr. J. C. Crawford. About a thousand parents and friends gathered in the body of the ball. Mr. F. S. Tim- mis, J.P., occupied the chair, and he was supported it), the Revs. J. Wrlght-Williams,Geo. The Chairman, in his opening address, declaimed that that was a political demonstration in any way, Mrs. lids. pratt, who took a great interest in educational matters, and had presented a handsome water fountain to each Board school, promised to distribate the prizes six months ago, when Mr, Mlnprates candidature was not.thought of. He remarked with gratification upon the sticoess of the labours 'of the Council. He announced that aimilar prizes would be awarded next year, and said before the end of next year the I system the Council intended to ttdopt in future years would be made known. .

lir H W Deacon, hon. trec , presented the directors report, i which stated that they re-elected Mr T Sutton Timmis as 'president, and eletted Mr R H Davis as vice-president, and the following-named gentlemen .:—Revs T Finegan and J Wright-Williams, Masers Deacon, Handley and Timmis as the Executive Committee for the second year. It was decided 1 that the system of prizes and certificates, which had been In operation during the first year, should remain in force during the get ond. The results are as follow :—St. Bede's 58, St Luke's 51, St. Mary's 138, National 152, St. Patrick's 149, Simm's Cross Board 428, Warrington Road Board 131, West Bank Board 288. The total number of prize-winners last year was 1,136, whilst this year the num- ber is 1,395. The directors considered that the system of prizes was producing a good effect on the attendance of the majority of the children, for it was especially satisfadtoty to notice that not only was the number of prize winners considerably increased, but that the average attendance was decidedly improved. In 1883 the average attendance is all the schools in the township was 75.5 per cent., in 1884 it was 79.5 per cent ,in 1885 it was 83 per cent. It was also satisfactory that a large proportion of the children who gained bank-hooks last year are still in possession of them. The scholarship grants have been maxis to the parents of each of the two boys who gained the free scholarships at the Famworth Grammar School last year, As boys attend- ing the linman Catholic Public Elementary Scho..ls in the township de not compete for the free scholarships, the directors accepted the offer of the honorary secretary to provide funds for one scholarship, to be competed for by such boys, end to be gained if any such boy entered for the Free Scholarship Examination and took a place entitling him to a scholarship. Sir Richard Cross declared that there was not the slightest intention to introduce non-elected members into the local couecils. He was glad to hear that the Tory party, Lord Salisbury, and Sir Richard Cross, were making progress, because when ! they were in power they had an opportunity of 1 bringing in a County Boards Bill, and did they do every- thing to put the representation of county boards in the bands of the ratepayers ? Not a bit of it. They brought in a bill in which county justices would constitute two- thirds of the board. Sir Richard also took him to task about the rates, and said" Mr. Muspratt also talked about the !rates, and said the farmers were very foolishly grumbling lat the rates they had to pay." He never said anything of the kind. What he said was that the farmers were very I foolish in being misled by the Torieeas to the remedy. "Mr. Muspratt." said Sir Richard," proposed to put the rates on , the landlord, or else to divide them half and half between , the landlord and tenant." That was perfectly true. He proposed it, but it was not in his Radical proposals. It had been the proposal of Mr. Gladstone, Mr. Gosched, and nearly every member of the Liberal party. (Applause.). , Sir Richard continued," All he would say about that was thet wheel they were telking about the quereion of the bur- dens no the land, if all the rates were put on the landlord, ! or if they were divided, the tenant would have to pay ex- actly the same amount, because if the landlord had to pay ' them the rent would be higher." As that was the assertion of a Cabinet Minister, he would like to test it by a great au- thority on political economy, J. S. Mill, who said, A tax on rent falls wholly on the landlord. There are no means bywbich be can shift the burden upon anyone else. It does not affect the value or price of agricultural produce, for this is deter- mined by the coat of production in the most unfavourable ' circumstances, and on those circumstances, as we have so ;often demonstrated, no rent is paid. A tax en rent, there- forts, has no effect other than its obvious one. It merely takes so much from tbe landlord and transfers it to the State." He would like to know if, after that, Sir Richard ' Cron still remained of the same opinion (cries of " Yes," ' and laughter). If so, it simply showed that the Tory party were determined to remain ignorant. If there was One thing more certain than another it was this: That we had over WI ' over again tried to tax personal property; we had tried it in this country and it had been tried in America, and had not ! succeeded. Speaking of the depression of trade, he thought • that never before had there been such a general depression throughout the world when this country had suffered so little. We had certain trades depressed at the present time —not all. Now he thought that he knew as much and more about the cause of trade depression as either Sir Richard Cross or Mr. Cottingham Moss, and he would undertake to say that Mr. Gladstone, the greatest financier of the time—(loud cheers)—was far more Cognisant ef the ' cause of that depression than those gentlemen who flouted him and sneered at him. ("Shame.") No man ever did greater things towards increasing the trade and prosperity of this country than Mr. Gladstone. (Cheers.) When trade was depressed in former times, the Liberals took off all re- strictions from it. but what did the Tories now propose to , do? They were about to put these restrictions on again ? What could be more ridiculous? Mr. Cottingham Moss said he would take the duty on tea, but would pa it on manufactured goods coming into the country. The worth of all the goads which were really manufactured and brought into the country was only somewhere about thirty millions out of a total of 426 millions. And yet out of that Ibe proposed to raise four or five millions of taxation. His (Mr. Musprattes) remedy for the depression of trade was the reform of the land laws. Let them remove the depression Of agriculture and they would remove the depression of trade. He thought his remedies far better than those of Tories, and if they would only return the Liberal party of power they might be perfectly certain that these I remedies would be carried out. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) He was epposed by a gentleman who, he could not help saying, intended to support a party which had always keen opposed to reforms In the past. At the present time they simply said they had carried out in a half-hearted manner ;the reforms which the Liberal leaders proposed. He asked his hearers to judge between these two great politics, and to return him, as a representative of the great Liberal party, with a handsome majority. (Cheers.)—A vote of conridence in the candidate was then moved by Mr. ENOCH HARVEY, seconded by Mr. GRIFFITHS, aad after being supported by Mr. Wm. Oultun, carried. An overflow meetinw was held in the Russell-road School- room. Mr. Timmis presided, and the meeting was addressed by the candidate and other gentlemen. MEETING AT FARNWORTII. On Wednesday evening, Mr. Muspratt addressed a crow- ded meeting of his supporters in the Old Grammar School, Farnworth, near Widnes. The chair was occupied by Cap- tain Brunner, and he was supported on the platform by Dr. Hurter, Captain Wareing, Messrs. John Brock, J.P., E. K. Muspratr,J.P., B. Brown, J. Lewis, E. Carey, T. Robinson, I H. B. Shores, &c. Mr. Muspratt, who was received with cheers again and ,again renewed, referred to disestablishment, and said what- ever view a man might take of the Establishment, whether be was in favour of its continuing to exist, ot its abolition, or in favour of the reform of the Church, as he knew the chairman and Mr. Brock were, it was perfectly clear to all that we were not prepared to deal with such a great politi- cal question. (Hear, hear.) He (Mr. Muspratt) said dis- tinctly that a question so momentous, so important, and carrying with it such great results for the good or ill of this gloat country ought to be placed before the electors as a direct issue at the election. (Cheers.) He had no objection to the question being discussed by the people while Parliament was sitting, but be said that to bring it before the electors at the present time without preparation was unwarranted i , and undesirable in every way—(cbeers)—and if he were re- turned to Parliament he should oppose by every means in 1 his power the question of disestablishment being brought before the next Parliament. lie maintained that such men as the late Bishop Fraser had done more to secure the Church eat iblishment than all the political partisans whr had been speaking upon that question, and had said Lb' eee 'would defend it. Nay, more, those who made the Chi- „ea question a party question before the Church WAS ab i so, ,ore attacked were doing the greatest harm to the,eears.rtlYvicittuies regard to C(ChhnereV rates No education, he thought that school fees should, were sooner abolished. become(ch 1 and that the deficiency below the amor abould be made up out of the Consolidated "Right you are," and cheers.) That was r Ala 'only way in which he thought the thing could be Jne, end done with justice to voluntary schools. (Cheers.) d• o .f (. the grant A. vote of confidence was passed. Last night a meeting of the friends and supporters of Mr. E. K. Muspratt took place in the Liberal Central Com- mittee-room. The room, capable of accommodating 500 ' ' persons, was crowded. Mr. E. Carey presided, and Os the platform were Dr. Hurter, Captain 11. Branner, Messrs. J. - mmeltsedhuacdatiobneewnitmhoaudterethliagtionsu. Morrison, F. Heyes, and Hampden Jackson (editor of the Financial Reform Almanac.) ,The CHAIRMAN, in opening the proceeding, said a great .07n3 necessity a t a t Free Education, as it was called, was introduced it would heard it stated in the pulpit the other day that it "Hoseinhgadlarilasoh would mean the relinquishuaent of their parental control arid responsibility. (Shame.) Dr. Hur- ter, who had knowledge of the working of free schools in Switzerland, would deal with this subject. (Applause ) Ha had beard there were some electors who did not clearly undersrand Mr. Muspratt's assurances upon the subject of Disestahlishment. Mr. Muepratt had over and over again stated that he consalered that this Parlia- ment was not being elected by the people of England for the purpose of even discussing the subject of Dieestabliah- mem-, and that so far as he was concerned, if he was elected, as he (the chairman) believed helwould be—(ap- pleuse)—he would not only vote against the subject being treated in this Parliament, but agaiest the subject even he- - Mg discussed. (Applause.) Mr FRANCIS HEYES moved a resolution pladging the meeting to use every legitimate effort to secure Mr. Mee- pratt's triumphant return. Tne reason why land was lying idle in Widnes was that the laud owner wanted a great deal snore ground rent for permission to live and toil upon the land than anybody could afford to pay him. (Hear, hear,. and applause, and a voice: "Shan.') Forty years ago that land could have been bought for £5O an acre, consider.= ably less than 3d per square yard. Now ihey demended Is per square yard. That was just four times the real and intrinsic value of the lard. (Applause.) Work would be scarce and wages low until this monopoly ef land was regu- lated by law So that the landlords could not cbaae.e more than a fair price. The Tories would never improve the land laws. and if the working-men voted for the Tories they would never obtain their natural rights. (Applause.) Dr. HOMES, who was well received, seconded the motion. Mr. Muspratt. he said, was a far more fit and proper person to represeat them than Mr. Tom Cottingharn Edwards-Moss. He had known Mr. Muspratt for a considerable number of years, And he had come in contact with him on various oc- casions, and be was doing no injustice to his own firm when he said that Mr. Muspratt was without exception the most educated and the most advanced of the alkali manufacturers of Widnes. (Applause.) Dealing with Free Education, Dr. hurter said it did net mean education for which they did net pay. It did not in Swi'zerland; there it meant that every man paid according to his abilities. (Cheers.) He had been brought up under a sysann of Free Education, and it was owing to that syetent that he, the son of a poor widow who had to work for her living was able to stand before them that night—(prolonged cheer)—a doctor, and fulfilling the conditioniand requirements of his profession in, he thought, a tolerably efficieet manner. (Renewed cheers.) His experience of free education was that it was not an education without religion, nor an education 'that would , lower the statue of the parents. On the contrary it was an education which in Switzerland at any rate was as earnest in religion as any of their schools in Widnes. (Cheers.) He had in his hand the certificates of his little boy and little girl, stating Hit subjects they studied, and at the head was the word "religion.' (Cheers.) The teachers belenge ing to the various denominatioes were paid by the State all alike for the same kind of education, whether it was a Catholic or a Protestant school. (Cheers.) He earnestly hoped they would return Mr. Muspratt to Pare harnent so that he might help them to get, not free educa- tion, but, as he preferred to cill it, " cooperative educa- te:in '—an education which would enable them to intelli- gently follow their trades and businesses. (Cheers.) Mr. HAMPDEN JACKSON then exposed the fallacies of Protection in a_capital speech.

' • The nomination of the two candidates for the re- presentation of Warrington in Parliement took place on Monday at the -Town Hall, and was of a purely formal character, There were present the ' Mayor (Alderman 'Harrison), who has acted through the election as returning officer, Mr. Wm. Crosfield (the Liberal candidate),. Sir Gilbert Greenall (the Conservative candidate), I , nd Messrs. 'J. G. 'Mc- Minilies William Beainont, Charles Broadbent, John 1 Peers, John Burgess, Robert Davies, Captain lisYnolds, William PierpOint, William Mertimer, John Roberts, William 11. Brook (tOwn clerk), Charles Cherley (borough treasuivir), and J. ,L. Whittle (deputy town . clerk), Mi. A. Browns Liberal election agent), and Mr. Henry Greenall Conservative election •agent.) Mr t William Cros- eld, 16, Alexandra 'Drive, Prince's Park, Liverpool, described as "Esquire," was proposed by Mrs John Gordon McMinnies, and seconded by Mr. John' Bur- gess, the .ftelowing gentlemen having subscribed the nom nation. papers, viz., Messrs. Charles •Brelielbent, ,Charles John Holines,Frederiek Monks, John Gree- ning, Edwin James Guest, William Pierpoint, Charles , Sawkins Burgess, and William Stirrup. Sir Gilbert Greenall, Walton Hall, Walton Superior, Cheshire, "Baronet," was• prctposed by Mr. Beamont, and. seconded by Mr. John Peersi • the following gentlemen having subscribed the nomination papers ;e-Messrs. Sylvanus -Reynolds, Robert True- man Smith, John Yineer,nt Taylor, Joseph. Davies, James Smethurst, Robert 'Wood Collin, Peter Stußs, and Robert. Greenall both,' stated that, they had no objection to make to the nominations, and the Mayor then declared that Mr. W. Crosfield and Sir G. Greenall were duly nominated. The pro- ceedings then ended, " • THE POLL. . On Tuesday morning the voting commenced at the variens polling stations .promptly at eight clock. The weather was of the most . disagreeable charac- ter, there being a steady downpour of , .rain which continued with little intermission throughout the •day. During the early- pert of the day little excite- ment waemanifeeted. but at the same time there 'was a steady flow of electors to the polling booths, and a considerable proportion of votes Were recor- ded by mid-day. Various sorts of private Vehicle i s were emPloyed n bringing up voters, and althoe.gh there was remarkably little display of party c'Oleur in connection with them, it was ;evident that the Conservatives, as usual, had the advantage in this ' respect. During the afternoon most •of the shops and other-places of business in the town were closed, and towards evening the principal streets of the town were filled with crowds, and the excite- ment became More and more intense as the time•for ' declaring the result drew neat Below we give a full aceceint of the Varioee incidents connected with the eleetoral contest. • • , • .ELECTION "LITERATURE. .' Trade, Education, and the Various matters affecting the Irish vote. • TITE •SITIP dANAL. * One of: the earliest placards put out was one by the Coneereatives claiming that Sit Gilbert had been an earnest supporter of the Ship Canal schema and showing that he had taken .21,000 worth of shares in the undertaking. This was met with the very effec- tive rejoinder that th 4 Conservative candidate had positively refused to allow his name to ,be put: on the Ship Canal COmmittee of promoters; that he had declined to subscribe a single farthing to' the first, second, and third applications to Parliament in respect of the canal; and that consequently he had "not given a fraction towards the costs of obtaining the Ship CanaL Bill, which had amounted altogether to the sum of £100,000." It was also pointed out that when the' ratepayers of Warrington almost unanimously agreed to levy , a rate of twopence in the pound toward the expense of promoting the Canal Bill Sir• 'Gilbert Greenall'e voting paper was returned' unfilled . up. "For th the e construction of e canal," continued this 'very caustic handbill,'" a,large portion of the Walton estate would be required, and for this land the pro- moters would have to pay Sir Gilbert Greenall the full market value, and ten per cent. in addition for compulsory sale, so that beyond receiving, the full price for his land he would be entitled to thousands of pounds besides. 'Although the prospectus of the Ship Canal had been before the public for weeks Sir Gilbert Greenall never subscribed for a single share until Messrs. Rothschild, the great financiers, had guaranteed to the promoters of the Ship Canal to raise what capital was necessary to carry out the scheme." The very obvious moral that was drawn from all this was " that from first to last Sir Gilbert Greenall had not placed a single penny in this great scheme until all risk of loss had. vanished, and he was absolutely sure of making a large sum of money out of the undertaking." This Liberal re- joinder as tc; the Ship Canal seemed to have been singularly effective, fer towards the close of the contest comparatively little:was said about the sup- port Sir Gilbert had given to the scheme. Some attempts were made' to' prejudice the elec- tors against Mr. 'Crosfield on account of his be- ing a member of the Liverpool Dock Board which had opposed the canal scheme, but Mr. Crosfield promptly pointed out that this opposition had been initiated some time before he became a member of the Board, and that, besides, he was not a mere repre- sentative of Liverpool's interest on the Dock Board, but that he was one of those who had been nomina- ted'by tke Board of Trade to watch over. ' the interests of the extensive mercantile and manu- facturing industries of Lancashire and neighbouring' counties, which were affected by the control of the Liverpool Dock Board. With regard to the canal, however, the tables were completely turned upon Sir Gilbert by a somewhat clumsy attempt to bribe the electors, by offering to give his first ten years' dividend of his £l,OOO invested in the Ship Canal to the Warrington Infirmary. In doing this he very seriously prejudiced the prospects of the canal un- dertaking, by saying that although he were to give, the Infirmary the first ten years' dividend, he did not think that institution would be one penny the richer for it. On the above questions ay great. dui of controversy has prevailed. the Irish and • Catholic 'vote, and especally Us, latter, being a wetter of doubt till, almost the day of election. P. O'Connor and, although a.resoln- tion was passed pledging- Irish electors to vote according to the desire of Mr. Parnell. it was guita evident fr-m the tenour of Mr. O'Connor's speech that the . .
