Parnell would be directed toeyote for the Tory candidate ; and within a 'day or two aWnieructions to this effect were given by, the Irish lesderel./ ; Pespiritel, ind;ridt alyieltis very serupelous, e2orts were put forth by . the Conservatives to make sure of. the Irish vote., They issued extra from the Irish manifesto above referred to and from Spent* made by Irish leaders which they thought told in favour of theiteown party, and in addition to this, to quote one glar- ing instance, they attrenpted to deceive the Irish electors by putting out a garbled quotation from a speech of Mr. Crosfield in which he explained that the word "Tory "was originally derived from a word signifying an Irish robber. -This attempt to mislead was, however promptly and effec- tively met by the publication in full of the passage in Mr. Ctosfield's speech which had been unfairly manipulated: An effective use was made by the Liberals Of the scathing comments Mr. Michael Devitt, one of the noblest and most single-minded of 'lrish patriots on the Tory party. "Mr. Davitt,". it was said, "speaking in Glasnevin Cemetery on Seand# last on the occasion of an annivers try pelebrationin,honnor of the Manchester martyrs (Allen, Larkln;and' pauld) said it was a humiliating thing that Iriah voters' In Great Erike ain were being asked for political reasons to pupport the brutal and cowardly and butchering Government Which im- brued its hands in the blared tif these men." A skit which excited the livelkeet interest bed reference to the fact that Sir Hilbert.Greinall we's 'specially patronised by the Orangemen, .and was in the following terms: " Orangemen of Warrington! :At this important crisis in the history of the country, vote for Sir .Gilbert Remember, William Prince of Orange, of " Pious and immortal memory ;" the battle of the toyne'; and no surrender." This placard was issued in the Tory colour, and for a time was accepted by some of . them as genuine, and, we have reason to 'oelieve, was put up in the Conservative Club as a bill issued by the party. It; however, gradually dawned on the some abet slow Mind of the Tory that there was something wrong about this blue placard, and towards evening a counter announcement was issued stating that the placard was a " Rsdical concoction." Desperate efforts were put forth to secure the Catholic Vote for the Conservatives, and numberless placards and hand-, bills were issued with this end in view. To meet these, efforts the Liberals gars prominence to the letter from 111t.t John Yatee,, ef LWerpool, which was read at the Liberal meeting on the Wednesday previous and .giveriin full in our last issue. Mr. Yetes stated There are few now living wbo have had greater experience than I baiter had of the acts 'and celidduct of the Libera party, and the deep sense of gratitude which! feel towarde them is, L hope and trust, Ittecirmighly impressed on the minds and hearts of all right- minded Catholics." A green tracelbill signed by One Irish Catholic voters, in which the' numerous votes in Par- Dement of Sir Gilbert Greenall antagonistic to the teterests of Ireland and Catholics were exposed. There has been 'some dispute as to one of, the signatures to , this handbill, and regal proceedings have been threatened in connection therewith. An attempt hes been made by the Conservatives to make some capital out of this affair, but not success- tally; as the Liberals have no fear as to the 'result of any action that might be taken from the' fact that they have witnesses who will justify them in the course they have taken with regard to the signatures. TRAPE, FINANCE, C. Some of the most interesting and attractive of the mura, literature had reference ta trade and finance. Some rather gruesome Illustrations were: intended to set forth the evil effects of Free Trade ; the alleged expenditure of £100,000,000 by .the late Government was severely descanted upon; and the evil consequences of Liberal Government were enlarged upon in no measured terms, and with an entire disregard of details and proof. The " retcrt courteous " in these cases was the issue of posters by the Liberals, in which it was pointed out that in 30 years the huge sum of £108,614,632 had been engulfed by the aria- blowy in England to feed them in ease and' indulgence to the great suffering of the middle 'and werking classes, and now the Tories wanted' to-rob the Poor man of -his cheap loaf by a cunning Rayal CoMmission echetne. Plac'erda Pub- lished by the Financial Reform Association were e also Circulated, e giving particulars as to the land from Which itappeared that 143 great landholders owned 21,167 square miles of land while 143 men owned land equal to more than one-third of England and Wales, and that since the year 1861 1300.000 agriculturalists had left the soil. On Saturday a handbill addressed to the working-men of Warrington, by "A Puddler," was issued. It pointed out that the Tories were trying to gull working-men of the town, but asked them to look at facts and not at words. The Tories were said "to he the knobstick employers in Warring- ton; to have done more than anybody else to reduce wages by employing koobsticks ; to pay the lowest wages of any firm in town; to have given the Roebuck job to Man- chester, when Warrington working-men were walking about with nothiug to do ; to buy their groceries and household goods from the London stores; to have withdrawn their subscriptions from the friendly societies after the last elec- tion ; to have called the ironworkers and the Irish electors insolent nicknames because they did not support Sir Gilbert Greenall in 1880;" and with incontrovertible force it pointed oat that the Conservative candidate, while preach- ing free trade, was the greatest monopolist in Warrington. "Au Ironworker" also made public a few whole- some facts. During the strike of 1881, he as- serted, When Sir Gilbert Greenall was waited upon he subscribed LI, but refused to pay more, although it was so much needed by the ironworkers at that time. Other gentle- men, Liberals in the town, doubled their contributions to the end of the strike. Again, by fixing the polling day on Tuesday the Tories deprived the working men of the town of about £1,850 in wages which sum would have been saved if the election had been fixed for Friday. THE POLLING ARRANGEMENTS. The arrangements in the different wards for the polling were most complete and seem to have been worked in the most satisfactory manner. The poll for the north-west district took place at the Drill Shed, Bath-street, where there were provided six polling stations. At the first divi- sion, the voters on the register, including lodgers, from one to 436, 437 to 893, 894 to 1.361, 1,362 to 1,858, 1,859 to 2,304 voted, and in division two from 6,604 to 7,030. The poll for the south-east district. was taken at the National Schools, Church-street, where there were three polling stations. Division one was reserved for voters on the register from 2,305 to 2,713. 2,714 to 3,108,3,109 to 3421; and division two, 7,031 to 7, 144. For the convenience of the voters in the norih-east polling district, the poll was taken at St. Peter's Schoolroom, John-street, where there were four stations, and also at the old Workmen's Club, John-street. At the first named place those en the register from 3,422 to 3,844, 3.845 to 4,253, 4,259 to 4,655, and 4,658 and 5,099 recorded their votes; while at the old Workmen's Club those on the list, from 5,100 to 5,504 and 7,145 to 7,594 voted. The Infant School, Cairo-street, was utilised for the south-west polling district electors, there being two divisions for voters on the register, from 5,505 to 5,830, 5,881 to 5,945, and 7,595 to 7,890. The Latchford district polling place was st. James' National School, St. James'-street. Latchford, where voters on the register from 5,946 te 6,326, 6,327 to 6,603, arid 7,801 to 8,030 recorded their votes. Where a voter was registered in respect of distinct properties in two or more townships, wards, or poll- ing districts, he was entitled to vote in the one he selected, but was debarred from voting more than once. The Liberal and Conservative committee-rooms were on the opposite side of the street. In number 1 polling station, in St. Peter's Schoolroom, the presiding officer in No. 1 booth was Mr. W. D. Draper poll clerk ; supernumeraries, Mr. Charles Cherley and Mr. John Fair- hurst, jun. The committees of the two parties were also accommodated in different parts of the same building. No. 1, including registered numbers from 2.305 to 2,713. presided over by Mr. S. Years• ley, poll clerk, Mr. E. Gibbon; No. 2, 2,714 to 3,108, Mr. H. J. Longton, presiding officer, Mr. Lvthgoe, poll clerk ; No. 3, 7,031 to 7,144, Mr. W. IL Draper. presiding officer, Mr. T. M. Draper, poll clerk. Neighbouring dwelling. houses were engaged as committee rooms for the respective parties. SOIITR•WEST WARD.—The polling station for this ward was at the Infant school, Cairo-street. The presiding offi- cers were Mr. Percy Davies and Mr. Thomas, solicitor, St. Helens ; and the poll clerke were Mr. R. Forshaw and Mr. ,C. Ainsworth. Neighlouriog dwelling-house were here also engaged as party committee-roems. LATCHFORD Weare—The polling station for this ward was at St. James's School, St. James-street, the committee room of the Liberals being at the offices of Messrs. Roberts, Dale, and Co., while the Conservatives were located in a neighbouring dwelling. POLICE ARRANGEMENTS.
Fortunately the services of the police were never required
Y,

during the day to maintain order in the town, yet adequate I precautions had been taken or any eventuality. In addi- tion to the local police force, under the command of Chief- constable Hunt and Inspectors Berry and Spinks, there were 40 county constables drafted into the town under the com- mand of Superintendent Weir, of the Warrington division, and Inspectors Mayo (Prescot), and Inspector Smith of the , Manchester division.

RESULT OF THE POLL. The doors of the various polling stations were closed promptly at eight o'clock. The boxes Were theo sealed by the presiding officer and conveyed with the utmost despatch to the Town Hall, where they were all deposited by a quarter to nine o'clock. The Mayor and Town Clerk imme- diately.set about the counting of the votes, assisted by the following gentlemen :—Messrs. Charles Sawkins Burgess, John Bprgess, Samuel Rigby Armitage, P. T. Winskill, John Gordon McMinnies, Frederick Monks, Ziba Armitage, Charles Broadbent. William Pierpoint. Henry Roberts, Frank Alfred Roberts. William C. Baines, Sylvanus Rey- nolds, John White, Thienry Appleton, Thomas Litton, John Ed wa.d Wright, Ebenezer James Hall, Richard Walker Francmnb, John Hampson, James Douglas Nekton, Wm. Sharp, James Smethurst, William James Burgess, and Ed- ward J. Nicholson, A few minutes after ten o'clock the Mayor came to the front of the Hall and announced the following to be the result of the day's voting, viz:— GREENALL (C) CROSFIELD (L)
Majority for Greenall

This announcement was received with mingled cheers and groans by the large assemblage which had gathered in front of the Hall, and was very quickly carried to every part of the town by eager messengers. SPEECH BY MR. CROSFIELD,

After the close of the poll the Liberal Club was quickly filled by persons who impatiently awaited the result, and the street in front of the Club was also densely crowded. After the receipt of the news Mr. W. Crosfield, who was present at the Club, addressed the crowd from one of the windows. On appearing at the window Mr. CROSFIELD was received with prolonged cheering. He said : I have to congratulate Sir Gilbert Greenall that he is now the member for Warrington. (iiisse..) He has beaten me; he has beaten us by 776 votes. Gentlemen, I have nothing to blame myself formn this contest. (Loud applause.) I have no reproach to cast on any single one of the friends who has given me his assistance durieg the contest. (Applause.) lam still a young man. (Applause.)l This is the first Parliamentary contest that I have engaged in, and I hope to live to fight again. (Loud and continued applause.) I hope to live to lead some Liberal constituency to victory. (Applause.) I grieve for you that, after all the exertion and •assistants you have given the Liberal party, we are on the losing side. (Hear, hear.) Ido not think this will be taken as a gauge of what is going on in other parts of England. (Hear, hear.) We are beaten but Liberalism will march on—(applause)—we shall still 804 Liberalism victorious, and though we have to watch from the outside of Pariiiment, we shall all of us rejoice in the victories which Liberalism will accomplish elsewhere. (Applause.) This is no time to speak long; but I could not refrain from saying this, and to thank everybody who has helped me for the help they have given the Liberal cause. (Loud applause.)

After the announceMent of a Conservative victory a scene of wild excitement was witnessed at the Conservative Club. Cannons were exploded on the bowling green, and a flag was run up. Sir Gilbert Greenell, accompanied by several leading Conservatives, appeared on the balcony facing Sankey-street, and were received with loud cheer- ing. Sir Gilbert Greenall, having very briefly thanked his- supporters, said they had won a great battle, and should another contest take place they would do it again. Short speeches were also made by Mr. R. Pierpoint and Captain Reynolds. Fireworks were "let off" from the Club, and there was an attempt to make a display of the word "Suc- cess," formed of gas jets, but, as it was blown out every minute or two, it was anything but a success. Thee streets continued crowded till a late hour. SIR RICHARD CROSS AT WARRINGTON. On Thursday eveu(ng the Rome Secretary visited War- rington for the purpose of conferring with a number of his supporters, and the visit was made the occasion for accord- ing him a reception, which took place in the Assembly, room at the Conservative Club. On Sir R. A. Cross, Sir Gilbert Greene'', and a number of prominent Conservatives of the district taking up positions on the platform, those present in the room, which was crowded, indulged in loud. cheering, which was continued for two or three minutiiil Mr. Bleckly, who was appointed chairman, referred to the success gained by the Tory party in Warrington, and asked the electors of the Newton Division to emulate that success by triumphantly returning the Conservative candidate. (Cheers.) They mast put their shoulders to the wheel and. do the work that the law required should be done on theit part in order to secure the election of Sir R. Cross, They must make their organisation as effective as had been. the

organisation that had secured the return of Sir Gilbert Greenell. and then they also would be successful. (Ap- plause.)—Sir R. A. Cross then gave a short address. He did not wonder, he said, at their assembling there after thel victory they had just attained to ,congratulate each other upon the example that Warrington had set. Ile was de. lighted to see his old friend (Sir Gilbert) in his proper place —(cheere)—which he was sure he would fill, not only with honour and credit to himself., but to the constituency. The first polling day was over. (Cheers.) They remembered the disastroue first polling day of 1880, but things were rath,r changed since then. (Applause.) He had every reason to believe that the boroughs polling that day would follew the example of the previous day. He was not going to talk politics to them. because it was quite clear they had decided in their minds which waa the right side, and had given very solid proof of it— (applause)—but he should like to thank his many personal friends, and friends of the cause, who had been working in his interest

in every part of the :Newton division, for the exertions they had made_ He mu.st also ask them to continue their exertions for a few days longer. If they would all work hard and corns to the pill victory would crown their efforts. " Coming events cast their shadows before," and the majority of 776, was not at all a bad shadow to have before him. (Aaoplause.) Let them try and beat even Sir Gilbert. (Laughter and cheers.) Their cause was a good one, md now that the storm bad been raised by the Radicals from one end of the country to the other, they would show them what Englishmen were worth. He had no objection to that party bringing their plans forward, he was obliged to them for it, for they had let it be known what they meant They had brought these plans forward, and, when the people would not have them, they had run away and left them. (Laughter and cheers.) Sir Gilbert Greenall, who was received with cheers, said that he was there primarily and almost solely to give the best helping hand he could to his old and valued friend Sir Richard Cross. England had long desired the opportunity that sad just been given it of discharging those men who had so neglected the trade of the country, 'and of expressing that England felt and desired that something more should be done than had been done towards the maintenance of the integrity of this country. Sir Gilbert next urged them to cordially support Sir Richard Cross.—The proceedings then terminated with the singing of the Pational Anthem, and afterwards the carriage of Sir Gilbert Greenall was dragged through Sankey•street by a number of his ad- mirers.

Take away love, and not physical nature only, but the heart of the moral world, would be palsied.—Sauthey. Smile not the legend as vain, that once in holy hands a worthless stone became a heap of silver. Let thy alchemist be contentment, and stone or ore shall be equal to thee. As they who, for every slight infirmity, take physic to repair their health, do rather impair it, so they who for every trifle are eager to vindicate their charactei, do rather weaken it.

If men were as ready to commend what they approve as they are to condemn what they disapprove, life would be rendered much more pleasant, and many thorns that now pierce men's hearts would never enter them. _ _ _

THE CONDITION OF IRELAND. NNW Somaron-Gumenswir. POR IRELAND -.Mr. J. Munroe, Q.C., Solicitor-General for Ireland, haying accepted an Irish judgeship, Mr. J. Gibson, Q.C., has been appointed his sue- ceesor. Mr. Gibson is Conservative candidate for the Walton Division of Liverpool, But his appointment to office does not interfere with his candidature. SutztlEE 07 lqugansts.—District Inspector Carter and a party of the Royal Irish Constabulary recently seized a tin box, containing a quantity of rifles, at "Fulaniore railway sta- tion. The box was addressed to a person in Tullamore, who, on being questioned by the polic-, denied having any knowledge of it. The affair has created much excitement in the town and district.

FREE FIONT ADA NATIONALISTS DINNER.—At the dinner following the National election convention at Tralee, a dis- turbance arose owing to a speaker referring to the recent murder of Mr. Curtin by Moonlighters. A free fight en- stied, and bottles and deCanters were used. Several re- ceived black eyes and contusions, and othere had to be eScorted home by their friends to escape further violence. AGRARIAN MURDER.—A murder has been committed on the Galtee Estate, war Mitcheltown. Edmond Tobin, a young mar, gamekeeper to Mr. Nathaniel Buckley, of Man- chester, had been missing for a day or two, and on Monday his body was found under a heap of stones on an eatate from which a tenant hae been evicted. Tobin had become un- popular in consequence Of acting in some suits instituted by his employer. An "Devierclntra" ter TROUBLEL—At Limerick, on Satur- day, Joseph Kelly, of Dublin, alias Brophy, stated to be a member of the Invincible Society, was chareed with being a rogue and 'a vagabond. It is stated he was connected with the murder of Lord Cavendish and Mr. Bourke, in the Phoeels Park, and a recent robbery of jewellery in Dublin, and other crimes. The accused was sentenced to six months' hard labour. i REctser, TO PAY RENT—AII the tenants on the exten- 'sive estates of Sir Richard Musgrave, In the County of Waterford, have refneed to pay their rents, as the reduction of 30 percent. demanded by them has not. been conceded. They have deposited the amounts due by them to their landlord, less the 30 per cent., in the National Bank to the credit of Mr. Jasper D. Pyne, one of the Nationalist can- didates for the country, and two of the lot leen belonging to parishes in which the tenants reside. Momentous AFFAIR IN DIIBLIN.—A man named Kelly I confessed to the Dublin police that he set fire to some thrashed oats at Thorn ville, oear Dublin, on Tuesday night, damage being done to the amount of £3OO. He stated he had been compelled to commit the outrage on pain of death. He belongs, he says, to a secret organisation, who directed ! him either to fire certain properties or shoot several persons whose names he gave. The decrees of the secret organisa- tion had made his life so miserable that he determined to give himself up for police protection. He refuses to divulge the title of the secret socley, or to give them the name of the man who met him by appointment and provided him with materials for giving the oath. SERIOIIS ELECTION RIOT.—A meeting was announced to be held on Monday at a place called Burton's Cross Road, about five mike from Dungannon, in the heart of a Protes- tant country, in favour of Mr. Mr. William O'Brien, the Nationalist cam-Ware .for South Tyrone. On the way to the meeting the speakers were met by a body of Orange- men, who stopped the brake and used threatening language. Stones were ;also thrown and sticks used, but no damage was done, the railings of the brake protecting itioccu- Pants. On reaching the field where the meeting was to be held, the Nationalists, hearing of the, attack on the speakers, made an attack on the Orangemen, and in the conflict which ensued Mr. Mulli!an, a poor-law guardi an, was shot in'the face and very badly injured. Great excitement pre- vai:s among the Protestant classes, as Mr. Mulligan ismuch respected.

Afire, causing damage, to the extent of between £l,OOO and X2OOO, broke out in, the Victoria Market, Oldham, en Mond ty morning. Nine million acres of land in Germany are devotA to the cultivation of the potato. The product last year amounted to 23,000,000= tons. Twenty-two persons have been ki led and upwards of 8.000 houses destroyed by a cyclone which passed over the Philippine lalmis on Hr. 7th inst. The infirmary at Sand uslcy, Ohio, was burnt down on Friday night. Of the 92 inmates all were rtscued, but five insane women, who were burnt to death. The superinten- dent was severely injured. The Melbourne Club will in all probability not send an eleven to England next season in consequence of an opinion having been lately expressed depreciatimg inclusion of five members of the last Australian team which visited England. The final decision has been postponed until Dec. 12th. MURDER ET A FATITER.—At Etherley Rene, near Bishop Auckland, on Sunday, John Young was fatally st tbbed by his father,. a butcher. Mr. Young quarrelled with his eldest son, and upon his younger eon John interposing he plunged a butcher's knife into the young man's abdomen. Death, ensued shortly afterwards. COLLAPSE OP A. Bonsulloor.—On Monday morning, the roof of an old house in Church-st., Heywood, occupied by a tailor named Simpson, and his wife and daughter, fell in. The occupants were in bed, and narrowly escaped with their litres.. When the roof fell in, it rested on the posts of Vse bed occupied by the sleeping couple. The house is now en- tirely unroofed. BARRISTERS—whose professional labours necessitate long lu• tervals between meals--nothing will be found 30 exhilarating, comforting, and capable of sustaining exhausted native as Cadbury's Cocoa, guaranteed absolutely pure.—Advt. DOIIRLS Exrictrrros'—John Willi tries and John Hill were executed on Monday morning, at Hereford Prison, for the murder of Ann Dickson at Weobley. An attempt was made to secure a reprieve for Williams, but without success, -.Berry, of Bradford, was the executioner, and be allowed a drop of eight feet. On the scaffold Hill bore him' self firmly, but Williams wept bitterly Death was instan- taneous.

Moors FOR INDIA.—Her Majesty's Indian troopship Crocodile arrived at Portsmouth on Monday, from Bombay, with the Indian reliefs. numbering 61 officers, 1,020 men, 56- officers' and soldiers' wives, and 105 children. Two deaths occurred on the voya,ze. Orders have teen received at Canterbury garrison to prepare 1,300 recruits •as soon as possible for India, to make up regiments to full strength. 'TRH MURDER BY ARMED BURGLARS The magisterial inquiry into the robbery of jewels at Netherhy, and subse- quent murderous assaults on policemen and murder of a comstable at Ptumpton was resumed at Cirliele on Monday. Some formal evidence was given, and the Chief Constable stated that that completed the evidence, Pelice-cone stables Johnstone and Fortune bein... still unable to appear. The prisoners Baker, Martin, and Rudge were committed for trial. THRRN PERSONS BURNT TO DEATH. A fatal fire oc- curred early on Monday morning at the house of Mr. G. Wintle, undertsker, 31, Georges-street, Cheltenham. It was discovered by a policeman, who heard a woman throw something from AN upper window to the pavement. The fire had cut off the means of flight by the stairs. A fire escape being brou,:•ht to the window, three children were found under the window burnt to death. Search is being made among the ruins for the husband. FATAL RIOT IN INDIA..—A serious riot occurred on Mon- day at Broach, in the Bombay Presidency, owing to an ascetic having failed to obtain a site required for building a temple. The rioters took possession of the arms at the police station, and proceeded thence to the Bank of Bombay, but were unsuccessful in their attempt to loot it. Mr. Prescott, the superintendent of police, was killed, and three men were severely wounded by the rioters, while five of the latter were shot dead by the police. Order has been restored. ATTEMPTED MURDER AT A BARRACKS.—At Birr military barracks the sergeant, when asleep in bed, Was awakened by a man who belonged to his company walking in the room, and on challenging him jumped out of bed just in time to escape a bayonet thrust, the bayonet being buried in the bedclothes It was quite dark, and a desperate struggle en- , sued, during which the sergeant was severely wounded by the bayonet. Being stabbed in four places, he called for help, and the soldier was arrested. The prisoner was con. fined in the guardhouse, but escaped by cutting a hole through the roof. He has been recaptured. ENCROACIIMENTS By LAWDOWNEISS Lord Bramwell having given a wholesale denial of the existence of com- mon rights, and asserted the rights of landownees to enclose waste lands on road sides, ,•as been taken to task. Instead of settling the question, his statement has brought out abundant evidence that Lord Bramwell is wrong and not even consistent with himself. Sir F. Pollock shows that in a famous case in which some of the inhabitants claimed common rights of fishing in waters owned by the Corpora- tion. Lord Bramwell gave a judgment that was quite in- consistent with his present repudiation of the rights of commoners, and both Sir F. Pollock and others have shown tkat there are open spaces still in existence in the neighbourhood of large towns that are being encroached upon illegally by landowners. Facts of this kind are enough to show the necessity for a better system of protect- ing the rights of the community against encroachments by lords of the manor and other landowners. ALLOTMENTS AND SMALL HOLDINGS.-4)n an estate in Hants, belonging to Mr. W. W. Beach, the system of al- Intments has continued with unvarying success for the last 50 years. There are on this property over 140 tenants bolding under two acres, and a large number more holding from two acres upwards, entirely of ;Ale labouring classes, who in the winter months find employment in the woods; and when summer comes a general migration of the district takes place te the corn and hop harvest fields, where labour is less abundant. The general rule is that the landlord pays tithes and rates; and this, added to, the agricultural value of the land, makes a rent that an industrious man finds no difficulty in meeting, evsn in these depressed times. The success of Mr. Beach's scheme is attained by the natural advantages of soil and locality, tor. on the other band, on a property of his situated on the chalk hills several allotment plots are lying idle for want eJ tenants, althvugh in the centres of populous villages. NI BARLOW'S CANDID.A.TURE.. THE INEQUITY OF TITHES. Below we.Pritit correspondence which has taken place between Mr. Barlow, the Liberal candidate for the Knutsford Division, and Mr. Thos. Turner' of Bollington, on the question of tithes. , It will be seen from Mr, l3arlow's lettettkat he more than jus- tifies the statement he made that tithes in some • cases , amount to more than the rent. lie furnishes instances where la4d'reMains uncultivated because the tithe charge sai heavy, that the land will not , Pay even if held rent free. It is a monstrous in- equity that this should be so, and, as the abolition of 'tithes is part .of 'Mr. Barlow's programme, we trust the farmers and farm labourers will vote to a man for him on •Thursday neXt, [corr.] 114(3E310j-road, Bolliagton„ ' • Macclesfield; 31st October, 1885. Trie Macclesfield Chronicle" you are reported as saying at Bainow Liberal meeting, on the 25th inst.. "He" (Mr: „Barloer) "could not see why tithes should amount to nibre than the rent, as was often the case." Would you kindly inform in. of a few such cases, giving the names and addresses of the farmers, with the amounts of rent and tithe respectively, which each bas to pay.-1 am, very respectfully years (signed) THOMAS TURNER. J. Emmett Barlow, Esq., Torkington Lodge, near Stock- port. ECOwr.] Torkington Lodge, near Stockport, Nov. 25th, 1885. thank you for your letter of the 31st October, 1885, asking me to mention a few cases in which the tithe Is more than the rent. I have before me a letter written daring the present month by Mr. James S. Gardiner. of Borley Lodge, Sadtatry, Suffolk, in which he mentions one farm which is let at 2e 6d per acre the tithe rent charge of Sc 6d per acre being paid by the tenant; also another farm of 300 acres let at Sc per acre, the tenant paying the tithe rent charge of 5s 6d per acre. He further mentions another farm of between 170 and 180 acres, the rent of which is .450 per annum, the tithe Sc per acre (which amounts to more than the rent) being paid by the tenant. In addition to tithes these tenants have to pay rates in the usual manner. But perhaps more striking instances are contained in a letter written to me a week or two ago by Mr. Joseph Smith, of Great Salink, Essex, he says :—" A farm of 365 acres, with a fair house and good buildings, now on owner's hands, liable to about £lO5 per annum for rates and tithe, will be let to any free of rent if they will take it, has been offered to me on these terms. Another 105 acres it let tO me by paying £lO per annum, and the tithes and rates which topount to 4,5) tithe end £l2 rates," Another correspondent writes to me from near Baty St Edmunds that: "From 9,000 to 10,003 acres of an estate not far from me,•belonging to his Highness, the Maharajah Dhuleep Singh, has quite gone out of cultivation; all the stock is sold off ; there is no employment for lahourera theie ;it does not pay to cultivate. Formerly this estate was held by skilled cultivators; they gave it up when it became unprofitable; the landlord took it in hand, and has lost heavily by it, so much so that he finds he will lose less money by letting it remain uncultivated." More Met:woes could be found, but these I deem sufficient. I have delayed replying to your letter because I was in- formed that von wished me to do so at a public meeting at Bollington. It now seems to be doubtful whether I shall attenel one there soon ; I am, therefore forwarding copies of these letters to the papers.-1 am, very faithfully yours, J. Emmorr BARLOW. Thomas Turner, Ent., Bollington.

div.head: MEETING AT KNUTSFORD.
div.p: MEETING AT KNUTSFORD.

A large and enthusiastic meeting in support of the can- didature in the Liberal interest, of Mr. J. E. Barlow, for the Knutsford Division was held in Knutsford Town Hall, on Saturday. Sir Henry Roscoe presided and made a few opening remarks, after which Professor Munro proposed, and Mr. George Hicks seconded a resolution expressing the opinion of the meeting that the speedy return to Parlia- ment of the Liberal party was earnestly required in the in- terests of the ceuntry.—The resolution was carried with cheers.—Mr. Barlow, who then rose to address the meeting, met with a heartfreception. The Tory party, he said, had raised the cry of the church in danger, and the big drum was being sounded to protect that estimable institution. Mr. Gladstone, they were aware' was pledged not to touch the establishment of the Church of England in the forth- coming Parliament. (Hear, hear.) Lord Harlington and Mr. Chamberlain were also pledged to the same. (Cheers.) Sir William Harcourt, he believed, had said something similar. He (Mr. Barlow) would not assist the leaders of any party to break the pledges on the faith of which they had been returned to power. (Hear, hear.) He would go further, and say that in his humble opinion any private ' member who should attempt to push that matter forward would be acting in a way which would be prejudicial to the Interests of the Liberal party and the welfare of the coun- try. The only effect of such action would be that we should have another dissolution of Parliament before they had effected those reforms upon which the Liberal party were all agreed, which the nation demanded, and upon the faith of the Liberal party accomplishing which they were about to be returned to power. (Cheers.) Therefore it was the duty of the Liberal party not to trouble with things they could not touch if they would, and which he, for one, did not believe they would have to touch ter along time, if ever. Mr. Barlow defended the Liberal Government from the charge of extravagance, and quoted figures to show that for a series of years they had carried on the Government of the. country at a much cheaper rate than the Conservative party. He then reiterated hie views on the land question, and detailed the reforms which he believed to be necessary in the intereets of tenant farmers and labourers. Their Con- servative friends prefeseed to be very glad they had got the franchise, and said it was just what they had wanted for is very long time. (Laughter.) Mr. Egerton, at oae of his meetings, bad expressed his gratification at seeing so many new electors, and when the Bill for their enfranchisement lOU before the House of Commons Mr. Egerton took the opportunity of expressing his opinion in a practical way by voting against it. (Hear, hear, and cheers) When he was asked at one of his meetings why he voted against the Franchise Bill no less than five times, Mr. Egerton said be voted against the Bill in order to enable it to pass. (Laughter.) He (Mr. Barlow) would suggest that the electors follow Mr. Egerton's example, and vote against hies in order to enable him to get into the House of Commons. (Hear, heart and cheers.) The new voters would expect that their representatives should look after their interests. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Egerton pro- fessed to he solicitous for the welfare of the newly-enfran- chised classes, and in a speech he delivered at Higher Never contended that it was better that the wealth of the country should be in a few hands, because the wealthy classes were willing to utilise their wealth for the benefit of their poorer fellow subjects. He (Mr. Barlow) believed the working clime did not wish to be depeedent on the caprice or the doles of charity of the rich. (Cheers.) What they wanted was a fair field and no favour—(cheers)—just and equitable laws, and houses fit to live in. Those and other neeessary reforms they would obtain by returning a Liberal Government to power, and on that ground he ap- pealed for their support. (Cheers.)—A resolution ap- I proving the candidature of Mr. Barlow was passed, on the motion of Mr. Winer, seconded by Mr. J. T. Brunner, Liberal candidate for the Northwich Division, and sup- ported by Aid. Thompson, Mr. W. Long, and Mr. W. B. Hocklehurst.—Mr. C. Broadbent proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman, which was carried, and the meeting terminated.

" That's too bad," cried her mother, " but won't soap and turpentine take the stain out ?" The amenities of American public life still remain our choicest model. A candidate lately spoke contemptuously of the recent date at which his opponent "first saw the light"—alleding, ef course, to his birth. The retort was— "lt is impossible to tell at what date my honourable friend first saw the light, though we know when he was born. I an not eaough of a zoologist to know how long it is before puppies of his class open their eyes." DOMESTIC MUSIC.— • I tell you, Bromley, I've married an angel." "Oh, no doubt! Walt until you've been ' married as long as I have." "She's all smilee, Bromley—never a cross word. Her voice is as sweet as the sound of a harp. Her—" "Oh, she reminds you of a harp, does she? Within a year she'll remind you of an accordion." "Why of an accordion ?" "Because she'll make the most noise when you attempt to shut het up." A temperance missionary in Glasgow left a few tracts with a young lady one morning. Calling at the same house a few days afterwards, he was rather disconcerted at observing the tracts doing duty as curl-papers en the head of the iamsel to whom he had given them. "Wee], my lassie," he remarkeu, "I see you have used the tracts I left wl ye; but," he added, in thee to turn merriment into eon- fueion, "ye have platen them on .the wrang side o' your held, ma woman !" Art ASSOCIATION OF IDEAS.—YOULhfIII masher, speaking to a lady who is playing on the piano: "Can you explain why it is that sentimental music always makee me think of you ?" Young lady: "No, lam sure I cannot. But it seems to affect me in the same way with respect to yourself. for I never hear & sentimental air but it always reminds me of you." Masher, with one of his killing smiles: "Indeed! And what can there possibly be in sentimental music to cause you to think of me ?' Young lady: "I don't know, unless it is because it is always soft." FAMILY SECEETEL—" Pap wants A new strap for that bridle he got here last week," said a small boy to the harness man. "H. hasn't wore that first one out, has he 2" Inquired the dealer. "Yes, sir." "What the mischief has he been doing with It? That strap ought to last a couple of years." "It don't make any difference wot he's been doin' with it," said the boy, clinching his hands behind him; "he wants another strap, an' if you think I'm goin' to give away family secrete, between pap an' me, you're mighty mistaken, and don't you forget it neither. Gimme that strap, for papsaid It wouldn't be healthy for me to stay away all day." HE Toox THE HINT AT LAST.--a I 'WM you were a fly," said a Brooklyn girl to an Anglomaniac slim who didn't knew enough to go home when the young lady yawned like a chasm. "Goodness gwacions !" he squealed, " that would be awfully jolly, don't cher know? I could make believe you were a lump of sugar, and—" "No, you wouldn't" she said. "The reason I wish you were a fly is because when.

that Intelligent insect maces a move io go he generally jumps two hundred tides his own length. Just make believe you are a fly, please." Then, and not till then, did he fly. In the troublous days of 1848 a curious communication reached an English morning paper. The French Revolution was a fait accompli, and no one could say how widely the conflagration would extend. Thrones were tottering from St. Petersburg to Madrid. The King of Prussia was in par- ticular thought to be in dangerous straits, and the enter- prising paper had a confidential agent at the capital, with Instructions to telegraph the impending fall of the monarchy the moment it took place. Late one night came the fateful message "The king has gone to pot." This was colloquial but emphatic, and a leader was written commenting on the new downfall among ancient monarchies. Early the next morning cime another message containing the cabalistic letters "edam." This was, alas, the conclusion of the first message, dislocated in the exigencies of imperfectly-ad- ministered telegraphy! The King of Prussia, it seemed, had only gone to Potsdam.

It is stated from St. Petersburg that preparations are being made for the mobilisation of two army corps. Lord and Lady Salisbury left Windsor Castle on Friday morning for London. . The Prince of Wales left London on Friday morning for Birmingham. A pension of .£3OO per annum has been offered to Pro- fessor Ilusiey, in recognition of his eminent scientific ser- vices. A Russian schooner was driven ashore on Thursday evening near Fifeuess, and the captain, mate, and three men wera.drowaed. Serious rioting is reported to have taken placeat Glaston- bury on Friday afternoon during the polling. The Mayor, in view of the serious aspect of affairs, read the Riot Act. , Loid Randolph Charchill attended at the India Office on Friday for the first time sitace his election for South Pad- dington, and was congratulated by the officials a the Department. FATAL COLLIBEY ACCIDENT.-00 Thursday night a waggon broke loose at Aston Hall Colliery, Llawarden. Three men were coming up the gig rope upon which the waggons are worked. At the time the waggon was heardap- proaching at a terrific rate two men jumped aside, but the third, Samuel Davies, of Penvinvoydd, Ilawarden, was caught and killed instantaneously.

Cooke (C). 3,s47.—Clapham Division : J. F. Moulton (L), 3,976; Hon. A. Bourse (C), 3.650. NOTTINGHAM.—East Division: A. Morley (L), 5,239; H. F. Hatton (C), 4,218. South Division: J. C. IRELAND. ARMAGH (SOUTH) —Alexander Blaine (N). DOWN (WEee).—Lord Arthur Hill (C). , GALWAY (Soone).—David Sheehy (N). MEATH (Nourn).—Dr. Kevin lead O'Doherty (N). Mae° (Easr).—John Dillon (N). ANALYSIS OF RESULTS. LONDON, FRIDAY, 3-30 PAL—The results of Thursday's elections, which were declared up to this hour this after- noon, show that there have now been returned to the new Parliament 119 Conservatives, 116 Liberals, 12 Nationalists, and 2 Independent Liberals, and the total number of votes polled has reached 6,58,770 for the Liberals, 658,728 for the Conservatives, and 10,362 for the Nationalists. The whole of the four divisions of Belfast have returned Conservatives, two of them electing the Orange candidates there—an Orangeman and a Conservative in each division. London- , deny lute also returned a Conservative Loyalist, and Mr. Justin McCarthy, the Nationalist candidate, Was defeated. The two divisions of Kensington hears each returned a Con- servative, and the two divisions of Battersea and Clapham each a Liberal. The Conservatives have won *seats at Scarborough and Wednesbury. It is stated that at the East Wilts polling booths on Fri- day many farmers acted as personation agents, and that the conviction produced thereby on the minds of the agricta- tural labourers was not in favour of the secrecy of the ballot ROSSENDALE. The polling foe the Rossendale division opened yesterday morning, and waa proceeding briskly, but in very un- pleasant weather. The candidates—Lord Bartington and Mr. W. F. Ecroy S--have held euesessful meetings in every part of the divieioo, and strenuous efforts are being made by both parties, a number of private carriages being em- ployed. There are 11,450 electors. MIDLOTHIAN. The polling at Midlothian wee taking place yesterday. Some advanced Liberals threaten abstention, but great efforts are being made to secure a. full poll. The result of the poll will not be declared until early on Saturday morn- ring or early in the afternoon. Mr. Gladstone, who is in good health, has visited some of the polling booths. To-day he will drive into Edinburgh shortly after two o'clock, and deliver an address to the members of the Rosebery Club Afterwards he will address a meeting of working•men in the Corn Exchange, and leave Edinburgh for ilawarden at five minutes past six. EDDISBURY DIVISION. Friday was fixed for the polling for the Eddisbury Divi- sion of Cheshite. The candidates are Mr. Lawrence Irwell (L), and Mr. H. J. Tollemache, who before represented West Cheshire in the Tory interest. The Tory voters in the division are very numerous, and the fight will be a stren- uous one. The voters number 10;346. Latest reports from the polling booths announce that the votes are being re- corded gradually.. Several feehicles are employed conveying 'electors, and patty colours are exhibited. Mr. Irwell's sup- Iporrers are sanguine of success. The votes will be counted to-day at Chester.

TRINITY CLOCK. Sir,—Will you allow me briefly to explain that the stoppige of the Warrington,Town Clock last Sunday night arose from no more serious cause than a deficiency of oil, and partly, no doubt, from the recent cold weather having thickened what oil remained, and so clogged the wheels. As the 'clock was going again and indicating correct time be- fore eleven o'clock on Monday morning, no serious inconve- nience is likely to have been caused. Its time-keeping has never been more satisfactory than during the last six months. From May 10th to September 15th its errors in the time of striking the hour never exceeded 10 seconds, and from September 15th to November 10th kept well with. in five seconds. These statements are not conjectures, but facts, akertained by frequent and careful comparison of the clock with the Leigh tirne•signal. A trifling amount of regulation occasionally has alone sufficed to secure these satisfactory results, no alteration of the time having been re- quired. MONSTRATOR "THE FARMERS' FRIENDS." Sir,--The Tory candidates who are contesting the seats in this neighbourhood are asking us farmers to return thern as they are "out true friends." Now, a week since to-day I had given me a list of the Divisions in the House of Com• mons during the passing of the Agticultural Holdings Bill of 1883, and I find that there hays been 14 divisions on such matters as whether a farmer must be paid for all his improvements ; that his rent should not be raised on his own improvements; the law of distress and other subjects; all in my opinion of vital interest to the farmer, his labourers, and tradespeople as well. The farmer would have benefited by knowlog that when he had improved his holding his landlord could not raise his rent, and he could enjoy the increase of production, which, by his skill, energy, and capital be had brought about. The labourer would have profited because the farmer weulti have wanted more of his labour ; first, to make his farm produce more. and then to house and take it to market; the tradespeople, because better and higher class farming must have been better than this impoverishing style of farming that we are compellad to pursuerat present. It would have made more money, enabling us, our wives and families, to come ta Warrington on a Wednesday with a bit of our spare cash, and our labourers' wives too, purchasing many things which now we have to do without, the one for want of money, and the other for want of work. Now. I see my opinion must not he the opinion of our late M.P's., for Sir It. A. Cross has given his vote ten times against us, Mr. Alan de Tatton Egerton six times, Colonel Blachhurne nine times, the two Tallernache'e seven Limes. Poor Sir Gilbert WAS not there, orbs would have swelled their ranks, for he does not like his land laws made , for him. The Ground Game Act ls net of much good to his tenants wheo his Mende can kill 132 hares at Hatton in one day. As to the cattle plague rate, about which Mr. Egerton said so much at Grappeahall, I believe he only pays to two of his tenants what they can all legally claim. Sir It. Cross now makes the working-man his pet as well as the farmer. andl wAnts to see him in a comfortable house. What about our Irish harvestmen on in a loft, and without any fire? He must never have thought of blue; but then it is a landlord's jab I should' like to ask him, too, if he thinks the agreements between the trustees of the late Thos. Parr. Esq.. and their tenants give to the tenants the fair and reasonable compen.ation, which he voted against. Now I do not think I am a blind politician, and have not pur- posely omitted the votes they have given in our favour, for there are none. However, they have the cheek to come and aro( for our sapport, and how farmers can be so blind as to support such men is a great panes to yours, At., A FARMER.

NORTHWICH ELECTION: MR. VERDIN AND THE TEMPERANCE ELECTORS. Verdin most look upon the Runcorn teetotallers as muddle-beaded muffs," or be would not have insulted their intelligence by the trashy argument he recently ad- dressed to them at the Public Ball. He said he could scarcely believe the statement that he had beard that the teetotallers of Runcorn were going to withhold their votes from him—a fellow teetotaller; and claimed their support because he was a life-teetotaller. It is very gratifying to a teetotaller to meet with a fits-abstainer, and especially when, as very rarely happens, I'm is a candidate for par- liamentary honours; hut even a teetotaller can distinguish between personal habita,and public sets. It is possible for a teetotaller to do immense harm to the cause of temperance aeform, as a referenced° the history of the past 50 years of temperance work abundantly proves. It is not only possible but highly probable that if Mr. Verdin, teetotaller though he be becomes member for North- wich, that he will help to rivet the fetters of the drink curse more firmly upon us. And for the very simple reason that he will be at the beck and call of the ;Tory whip, who will laugh him out of his teetotal scruples and teach him to do nothing toalienate those firm supporters 'et the Tory party—the grog reonopolists and their minions. Mr. Bronner has promised to support the principle of 'Local Option to the extent of the dirtct popular veto, and that is all that we as temperance electors seek in a candi- idate. Mr. Verdin will not touch the question. He will ; Wait till the matter comes up in the House of COMMODB, and then give it his "most careful consideration." The tee- ; totallers of Runcorn have read their "Alliance News" too ; carefully and too often to be pat off with such ridiculous ; trifling as that. If Mr. B unner chooses to make a ; humourous allueien in answer to a facetious question re- specting the swindling practices of brewers, it makes him ;a no less tit representative of our views, but rather more fit, considering that be by se doing becomes a congenial follower of that inveterate joker, Sir Wilfrid Lawson. Mr. Verilin seems to be impervious to a joke, and he must be a lineal descendant of the man who had to undergo a surgical operation before a joke could be got inside his head ; for this is not the first of Mr. Brunner's jokes the Point of which he has failed ,to see. Seriously, Mr. Verdin has by his action during this contest put it out of the power of the true teetotallers to give him their sup- port. A Mr. Blatherwick, of Manchester, advertised as a work- ing man and a Conservative (rara (leis) has been employed by Mr. Verdin to help him at his meetings in various places in the division. Now, this Mr. Blatherwick is a dravman in the employ of one of the largest brewery firms Manchester, the head of which is a Mr. Chester Johnson. Is it likely that this brewer tellow would send one of his servants to help Mr. Verdin in his candidature if he was a candidate worthy of the support of the teetotallers of Run- corn, or anywhere else 2 Out upon such humbug ! Yours, kkc., A TEETOTAL POLITICIAN.
